#5475. We keep coaching real estate agents to be salespeople. That was never the job

OPINION: Lance Pendleton argues that real estate agents are consultants, not salespeople. Learn what to ask before you pay for a coaching program.

I was the national head of agent development at Compass, and I’ve been in front of more than 30,000 agents since. I’ve also sold the thing I’m about to take apart, so keep that in mind while you read.

Here’s the usual scenario: You sign up for a coaching program. You’re excited, and you should be. Everybody wants to feel a little less alone in a job you mostly do by yourself, in your car.

You didn’t fail the program. The program failed you. How come?

The reason is simpler than anybody wants it to be. Nearly every coaching program in this business teaches professional sales skills to people who are not in sales. We’re consultants, advocates, advisors and educators.

Nobody has ever talked a family into a house they didn’t want to live in. What we do is help people through the largest and most emotional decision of their lives with the least amount of damage. We read a room. We tell someone the truth about their kitchen, and we hold a deal together at 9 p.m. on a Sunday when the buyer’s father has opinions.

That is not selling. We’re consultants, advocates, advisors and educators. If you can fog a mirror, you can get a license. Very few people can do those four things well, and I’ve yet to see a program that teaches them as a skill set.

This isn’t the coach’s fault. Coaches were trained the same way the rest of us were. Build the database. Reach as many people as you possibly can. Add value, and then add more of it tomorrow.

There’s a word buried in there that I think is the dumbest one in our industry, and I say that with love. Value.

We all have the same value. Every one of us can pull a comp, open a door, write an offer and get to a closing table. What almost none of us have is a point of differentiation, the thing that tells a consumer specifically what you do for them and why it ought to be you. You can follow “add value” for a decade and stay interchangeable with the other four agents the seller interviewed.

There’s a second reason the homework never gets done: Agents live in two periods of time: now and not now.

Now is the pipe that burst three hours before a closing. Now is the appraisal, the inspection, the client calling at 10:30 p.m. about something that could have been a text. Now is loud, it’s permanent, and it pays this month. Not now is quiet and pays in three years, if at all.

The trouble is that everything producing long-term income security in this business sits in the not-now column. The National Association of Realtors’ 2026 member profile puts median gross income at $88,500 for agents with 16 years or more in the industry, and $8,000 for agents with two years or less.

The veterans report a median 49 percent of their business from repeat clients and another 32 percent from referrals. For the newest agents, both of those medians are zero.

Somebody will say that’s just arithmetic, that you need a past client before you can have a repeat one. That’s the point. The whole gap is 15 years of relationships, and not one hour of that work feels urgent on a Tuesday. This is a patient business being coached like an impatient one.

We do something else I think is worse. We coach in a permanent state of enthusiasm. Everything is fabulous; every market is an opportunity; you’re crushing it; this is your year. I call that toxic positivity, and it does real damage. You sit in a hard month with two deals coming apart, you hear all of it, and you quietly conclude the problem must be you.

What would help is unglamorous. This job burns through five things: prioritization, organization, time management, impulse control and emotional regulation. By Thursday of an ordinary week, most good agents are running low on at least two.

There’s nothing wrong with any of those people. Real support builds bumpers around those five, the same reason a bowling lane for kids has them. You don’t make the gutter disappear by concentrating harder.

That work means dealing with people as they are, for who they are. Not more, more, more. Not the next great thing. One thing, chosen for that person, small enough to start on a Thursday when everything else has gone sideways.

We haven’t served this business well on that, and I include myself. I’ve sold the four-week cycle. It’s a comfortable thing to sell, because Week 1 always works.

If you’re picking a program this fall, ask what gets cut. Anybody can hand you 15 things. The one worth paying is the person who tells you which one matters and which 14 you can skip.

We’re not in sales. We never were. Until the coaching in this business is built for that job, we’ll keep running very good people through programs that leave them feeling like the problem.

You aren’t the problem. This is still the best time there’s ever been to be a great agent. We just have to stop training you for somebody else’s job.

The views and opinions expressed here are those of the contributor and separate from the Inman newsroom.

Lance Pendleton is the founder of Reframe Lab, a coaching and consulting practice for real estate agents, and the former national head of agent development at Compass in Connecticut. Get connected on Instagram.

#5474. Astelia’s autonomous network mitigation blocks AI-driven exploits without a patch

Exposure management company Astelia Inc. today announced the launch of autonomous network mitigation, a new capability that allows organizations to block artificial intelligence-driven exploits at the network level, even when a patch isn’t available or can’t be applied.

The new capability has been designed to address what Astelia says is the problem of frontier AI models cutting the time to exploit to almost zero, leaving manual triage and remediation unable to keep up. Astelia argues that autonomous remediation isn’t a viable option for large enterprises, where every patch requires a change window so it doesn’t break important business processes. In many cases, there is also no patch to apply because the vendor hasn’t released a fix yet or, for older and end-of-life systems, never will.

“For years, security teams have been told to patch faster,” said co-founder and Chief Executive Alon Noy, adding that the advice “stops working when the exploit arrives before the change window does.”

Autonomous network mitigation is designed to block the path an attacker would use to reach a vulnerable system instead of changing the system itself. Mitigations are applied automatically within policies the organization sets. Nothing on the asset is changed, allowing business-critical systems, including operational technology, to stay online.

Underpinning the service is Astelia’s reachability analysis, which maps an organization’s real network topology and applies agentic AI to analyze the requirements of each exploit. By correlating exploit conditions with network topology, the platform identifies which vulnerabilities are reachable by attackers and through which paths. In one enterprise deployment, approximately 40 million vulnerabilities were reduced to fewer than 2,000 that were reachable, according to the company.

Key features of autonomous network mitigation include the ability to identify the most effective choke point on an attack path and drive the mitigation through an organization’s web application firewall or intrusion prevention and detection system. A single rule at a choke point is said to protect every vulnerable server behind it, compared with one change per server when patching. Because mitigations are only applied to paths that have been proven reachable, the service doesn’t add rules for exposure that doesn’t exist.

Every mitigation applied by Astelia can also be rolled back, something that isn’t always possible with a patch. That is said to allow teams to act quickly without putting business operations at risk.

Autonomous network mitigation can be deployed through Astelia Agents, the company’s suite of AI agents, as a dedicated agent that applies mitigations on its own. The agent can also be connected with other agents to respond to urgent threats such as zero-day vulnerabilities and critical disclosures. Astelia gave the example of the PHP2Shell remote code execution flaws disclosed in October, which left end-of-life PHP servers with no official fix.

Each organization sets its own guardrails on how mitigations are applied. Users can require human approval for specific environments or actions, according to the company. Every action is logged and can be audited. Analysis on the Astelia platform continues to run on read-only integrations, with mitigation actions using scoped permissions that each organization enables and controls.

Autonomous network mitigation initially supports web application firewall and intrusion prevention and detection rules, with support for firewall rules planned in the future.

Founded in 2024 by former leaders of the Israeli National Red Team, Astelia is a venture capital-backed company that raised $35 million in combined seed and Series A funding in February. Investors in the company include Index Ventures, Team8 and Holly Ventures.

#5472. Tech Roundup: Zillow Preview listings go live in RealScout

Can AI time savings be measured? Lofty is trying. Plus: $1.65 billion in October proptech funding, Airbnb’s AI travel agent and Zillow Preview in RealScout.

This week’s Inman Tech Roundup covers Lofty’s new monthly index, which tallies how much time its AI saves agents, a $1.65 billion October for proptech funding, Airbnb’s early-2027 launch window for its AI travel agent and Zillow Preview’s new home inside RealScout.

Lofty is launching the Lofty AI Index for Real Estate, a monthly report tracking how much time its AI tools save real estate agents. The inaugural edition found Lofty AI products, including Lofty Cowork, completed 1.13 million tasks in October, saving real estate agents 131,248 hours.

The index counts tasks Lofty’s AI completed, such as follow-ups, social media posts, homeowner check-ins and CRM updates, then estimates how long each would take an agent to do manually.

Among the findings: 387,824 leads got an AI follow-up text or email; solo agents saved 30 percent of their hours on daily planning; and agents in Michigan saved more time than any other region.

“Every AI vendor touts the time-saving nature of their AI product, but almost none of them show the data to confirm that what they say is true. We decided to cut through the smoke and mirrors around AI results and create measurable clarity with the Lofty AI Index. Each month we’ll put a number to the AI impact, show the calculations and stand behind it,” said Joe Chen, CEO of Lofty.

The time-saved figures rest on the company’s own estimates of manual task times, and the release doesn’t say how many agents are behind the totals, which makes per-agent impact hard to gauge. Since this is the first edition, there’s no prior month to compare against yet.

For real estate agents weighing AI tools, Lofty’s index is a step toward the kind of hard numbers the industry has been missing. It gives them a benchmark to press other vendors on when they make time-saving claims.

However, the most useful measure is their own: tracking whether hours freed up by AI actually turn into more conversations, listings and closings.

Note: Lofty is the official AI partner of Inman.

Proptech companies raised about $1.65 billion across 34 funding rounds in October, according to the Center for Real Estate Technology & Innovation (CRETI), which called it one of the strongest months of 2026.

The money was heavily concentrated. Construction and development took roughly $872.4 million, or 52.8 percent of the total, while residential pulled in $604.4 million, or 36.6 percent. Three deals alone accounted for nearly 75 percent of October capital: Bedrock Robotics’ $600 million Series C, Unlock’s $433.1 million debt financing and ICON’s $200 million Series D.

Debt was a big part of the story. About $588.6 million, more than a third of the month’s total, came through debt rounds. That includes Unlock’s financing for its home-equity agreement platform and CrowdProperty’s roughly $133.5 million round for residential development lending.

That means much of October’s residential funding didn’t go into software at all but into financial products tied to home equity and property lending.

CRETI noted that funding signals investor conviction, not proof of ROI, and said the bar for founders is rising to show a credible link between their technology and a material financial outcome.

The numbers suggest investors are betting less on new real estate agent-facing software and more on the expensive, physical end of housing, such as building homes faster and cheaper and financing the transactions around them.

If that capital pays off, the bigger impact on agents and brokers may come indirectly, through more housing supply and new ways for homeowners to tap equity, rather than through the tools on their desks.

Airbnb plans to roll out its AI travel agent to consumers in the first half of 2027, the company said in its third-quarter shareholder letter, firming up a timeline it had previously pegged only as sometime in the next year.

Instead of a text-heavy chatbot, the AI agent will assemble a custom interface around each guest’s request, pulling from hundreds of travel-specific components such as maps, photos, comparisons, calendars and itineraries. It will also handle post-booking tasks like reservation changes, refunds, rebooking and payment issues, which Airbnb argues outside AI agents can’t easily do.

CEO Brian Chesky told analysts that general-purpose AI agents are fine for routine tasks but not for trip planning.

“Travel is aspirational,” Chesky said. “Discovering where to go and where to stay is part of the experience.”

The announcement came alongside a strong third quarter for Airbnb. Revenue grew 19 percent year over year to $4.87 billion, beating Wall Street estimates. Airbnb raised its 2026 growth forecast to the high teens, up from the mid-teens. Chesky called it the company’s fastest revenue growth in more than three years.

Airbnb’s bet is one real estate portals and brokerages are weighing, too: that owning the search experience and the transaction behind it beats handing consumers off to general-purpose AI agents.

If a custom, visual AI agent wins over travelers, it’ll strengthen the case for real estate platforms to build their own AI home-search tools rather than relying on outside chatbots to send them buyers.

RealScout is now showing Zillow Preview listings from hundreds of participating brokerages in its collaborative home search platform, putting pre-MLS inventory in front of buyers searching with their own agents.

The integration, first announced in September, extends Zillow Preview’s reach beyond Zillow, Trulia and Realtor.com to RealScout’s network of more than 100,000 agents.

Preview listings appear in client searches and listing alerts that include Coming Soon properties. Buyers can message their agent directly about a home, and each Preview listing is replaced by its MLS listing once the home goes active. Agents and brokerages don’t need to opt in to see eligible listings.

RealScout CEO Andrew Flachner framed the move as a transparency play, with a not-so-subtle shot at private listing networks.

“Listing transparency comes down to whether a buyer can choose the agent they trust without worrying that the right home is hiding behind another brokerage’s velvet rope,” Flachner said in a statement. “With Zillow Preview listings from hundreds of brokerages now available in RealScout, agents can give their clients more of the market through the home search experience they already share.”

For agents, the integration means clients can see pre-MLS listings from participating brokerages in the search tool they already use, without signing up for Zillow or leaving the agent relationship. It also gives buyer’s agents an earlier look at upcoming inventory, which matters most in tight markets, where a few days’ head start can decide who gets a showing first.

#5471. Three insights you may have missed from theCUBE’s coverage of NetApp INSIGHT

Intelligent data infrastructure is becoming a priority as enterprises move artificial intelligence beyond isolated pilots and into production environments.

The shift places new demands on storage systems built to support traditional applications, especially as organizations introduce AI workloads across hybrid and multicloud environments. NetApp Inc. is responding with a strategy that emphasizes infrastructure modernization without requiring enterprises to abandon existing investments, according to George Kurian (pictured), chief executive officer of NetApp.

“I think that the AI era requires organizations to be really good stewards of their data, because data is the foundation for knowledge and knowledge is the intellectual property,” he told theCUBE. “To have knowledge, you need really good intelligent data infrastructure that not only allows you to extract memory and context from your data, but also to keep it secure, well governed and a resource that you can trust.”

Kurian spoke with theCUBE Research’s Christophe Bertrand and co-host Rebecca Knight during NetApp INSIGHT, in an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. The event’s coverage featured NetApp executives and technology partners discussing the evolving demands on enterprise data infrastructure and the challenges of bringing AI into production. (Disclosure below.)

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video discussion with George Kurian:

Here are three insights you may have missed from theCUBE’s coverage of NetApp INSIGHT:

Enterprise AI workloads are exposing limitations in storage architectures designed for more predictable application demands. NetApp’s Novus architecture separates data and metadata management so each can scale independently. The company’s AI Data Engine is designed to discover, classify and prepare enterprise data for AI applications, according to Syam Nair, chief product officer of NetApp.

“Performance and throughput of accessing the data, that’s a necessity for AI, but that won’t be sufficient for agents to actually act on the data,” he said during the event. “If the data is not ready and it’s not protected, you get fast results. You get compromised results, but they may not be the ones you want.”

The demands of AI factories are also changing how storage resources must be managed. NetApp’s approach aims to support high-throughput AI pipelines without sacrificing the responsiveness other applications require, according to Arindam Banerjee, chief platform and technology officer of NetApp, who spoke alongside Jason Hardy, vice president of storage technology at Nvidia Corp.

“What happens is [that] different types of workloads like transactional workloads for metadata and heavy sequential workloads for, say, checkpoints, happen at the same time,” Banerjee told theCUBE. “Previous architectures did one or the other very well. They never were able to combine it and do both at the same time.”

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video interview with Jason Hardy and Arindam Banerjee:

Modernizing enterprise infrastructure often requires organizations to accommodate existing applications while introducing new AI capabilities. NetApp and Oracle Corp. are addressing that challenge through a co-engineered, fully managed storage service that runs ONTAP natively within Oracle Cloud Infrastructure. The offering is designed to ease migration of existing ONTAP workloads without requiring application redesign, according to Konstantinos Papamiltiadis, senior vice president of partnerships at Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, a division of Oracle.

“When I’m going into the OCI console, I have the option to use the ONTAP as a native service,” he told theCUBE. “For me, the most important thing that we managed to build is, from an operational perspective, we bring everything under one single interface that provides simplicity and consistency.”

NetApp and Oracle Corp. are extending enterprise storage capabilities into the public cloud through a co-engineered, fully managed service that runs ONTAP natively within Oracle Cloud Infrastructure. The offering is designed to ease migration of existing ONTAP workloads without requiring application redesign, according to Konstantinos Papamiltiadis, senior vice president of partnerships at Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, a division of Oracle.

“When I’m going into the OCI console, I have the option to use the ONTAP as a native service,” he told theCUBE. “For me, the most important thing that we managed to build is, from an operational perspective, we bring everything under one single interface that provides simplicity and consistency.”

The integration challenge extends beyond cloud storage to the networking and compute resources that support AI workloads. NetApp and Cisco Systems Inc. are expanding their FlexPod infrastructure with validated designs intended to reduce deployment complexity. The partnership has served 10,000 customers over 16 years, according to James Cole, vice president of data center networking, business development, partnerships and go-to-market at Cisco, and Alvaro Celis, chief partner and ecosystem officer at NetApp.

“Twenty years ago, 10 years ago, you would’ve been designing your data structures and your applications around the infrastructure. Now we’ve turned that on its head,” Cole said during the event. “You’re really designing the infrastructure around the movement of data. Who better to do that together than the person you trust with your data and the person you trust with your network?”

Another partnership focuses on private AI deployment and measurable business outcomes. The NetApp AIPod Mini combines NetApp infrastructure with the Generate platform from Iterate Studio Inc., doing business as Iterate.ai, according to Brian Sathianathan, co-founder and chief technology officer of Iterate.ai. In one insurance deployment cited during the discussion, an agent reduced accident-report analysis from approximately eight hours to eight minutes.

“AIPod Mini has attached connections to the NetApp storage, and it talks to NetApp using the ONTAP protocol that’s time-tested,” he said during the event. “Then, on top of the AIPod Mini, we are running our Generate software. That software has a [large language model] embedded in it, so you can run all your AI queries locally and fully privately within your four walls.”

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video discussion with Alvaro Celis and James Cole:

As enterprises introduce autonomous agents into infrastructure management, intelligent data infrastructure must accommodate increasingly complex operational demands. NetApp’s unified control plane, delivered through NetApp Console, is designed to reduce routine administrative work through policy-driven automation. In one keynote demonstration, agents responded to a nighttime performance anomaly, according to Sandeep Singh, senior vice president and general manager of enterprise storage at NetApp.

“Agents can, in real time, implement the necessary quality of service rules to ensure there’s compliance to the boundary conditions there,” he told theCUBE. “And that way, no human is woken up. The right outcome is achieved, and there’s no noisy neighbor effect. And there’s an audit trail presented to the humans for going and following up.”

Automation, however, can’t resolve organizational questions about data ownership and responsibility. As enterprises extend intelligent data infrastructure across applications and environments, leadership must establish accountability for the information those systems rely on, according to Helen Yu, founder and chief executive officer of Tigon Advisory Corp., who appeared alongside Singh.

“It’s not a storage problem. It’s a leadership and accountability issue,” she said during the event. “When teams don’t have access to … trusted data consistently, they actually stop making decisions. They start making workarounds.”

#5470. Existing-home sales sink to a 16-year low as mortgage rates bite

October was the perfect storm for existing-home sales, with a typical seasonal slowdown made worse by elevated mortgage rates, a worsening macroeconomic environment and political uncertainty.

Existing-home sales during October declined 5.5 percent month-over-month and 8.8 percent year-over-year to a seasonally adjusted rate of 3.75 million, the lowest rate since August 2010 (3.68 million). Annual sales declined in all four regions; however, the Northeast was the only region to also experience a month-over-month drop.

Despite slowing sales, unsold inventory (1.59 million units) and the median home price ($416,700) increased by 1.3 percent and 0.4 percent, respectively.

NAR Chief Economist Lawrence Yun said mortgage rates are the primary cause of current market woes.

Fixed rates experienced a rapid-fire ascent at the beginning of the fall, breaching 7 percent on Sept. 24 and then roughly a week later reaching a three-year high of 7.40 percent on Oct. 8. The catalyst had been two-fold: the Federal Reserve had hiked the federal funds rate (i.e., short-term rate) by 25 basis points during its Sept. 16 FOMC meeting and 10-year Treasury yields were rising at a historic pace.

Rates have since relaxed to the lower 7 percent range, but the short-term damage is already done.

“Homebuying is difficult when mortgage rates have climbed to their highest levels since 2000, aside from a single month in 2023,” Yun said in a written statement. “As a result, home sales fell to their lowest level since August 2010.”

Although Freddie Mac’s Primary Mortgage Market Survey saw rates drop for the fourth consecutive week to 7.11 percent, Bright MLS Chief Economist Lisa Sturtevant said she expects mortgage rates to start rising again in the coming weeks because of sticky inflation.

“There is little reason to expect rates to come down before the end of the year,” Sturtevant said in an emailed statement. “In fact, given this week’s inflation report, it is much more likely for us to see rates increase instead of decrease.”

Yun and Sturtevant said mortgage rates will continue to impact home sales — not inventory and home price growth.

“So far, we haven’t seen higher rates lead to widespread price declines. In fact, home prices are still rising in many local markets,” Sturtevant said. “Inventory is rising, but higher rates are holding back some sellers along with buyers. Because both sides of the supply-demand equation are slowing, it’s not likely for home prices to drop significantly, even if rates move higher.”

Added Yun, “It will be the highest inventory count since November 2019. We are now back to pre-COVID inventory conditions.”

Mortgage rate volatility has pushed homebuyers to slow down or pull out of the market altogether, as shown by September’s pending home sales, which declined 7.3 percent month over month and 11.3 percent year over year.

As a result, homes are sitting on the market longer, averaging 35 days. Most homesellers, Yun said, can wait for the market to turn in their favor, thanks to strong home price appreciation.

“Despite fewer transactions in October, the 88 million homeowners across the country are largely in a comfortable financial position due to sizable housing wealth accumulation,” he said. “The number of distressed property sales remains historically low at only 2 percent of all transactions.”

However, if a homeseller is in the position where they have to sell now, due to career or family changes, they’ll need to get comfortable with making a price cut.

“If the homes are not selling at the listing price, it requires a discount,” Yun said in a pre-report call Thursday morning. “The longer the days on market, the larger the discount. If the home is sitting on the market for more than 60 days, it requires a 9 percent discount … Even with this discount that is occurring, the median home price is still squeaking out a small gain.”

Yun and Realtor.com Chief Economist Danielle Hale said existing-home sales could improve in November and December — if mortgage rates continue to relax.

“Fortunately, the 10-year Treasury yield has pulled back from its early October highs, which has helped nudge mortgage rates below this recent peak,” she said. “However, several factors are likely to put a floor under how low rates can go.”

Hale said jobs and inflation trends will determine whether rates can move back toward the high sixes.

“[The] expected need for tighter monetary policy in the near term combined with sizable demand for capital from both governments and private companies, largely to finance AI-related investments [also matter],” she said. “Put simply, I expect to see more homebuyers come back into the market as we move away from recent mortgage rate highs, but the upside will be limited.”

Yun said rates below 7 percent could unleash a wave of untapped demand, allowing homebuyers to finally seize the advantage they’ve been given in terms of income growth, inventory and negotiating power.

“One wonders whether current price-declining markets will see buyers step in and stabilize the market,” he said. “We are not in a recession, and we are adding jobs. First part is prices, second is income growth. Wage growth is helping modestly on home affordability, but the big change is from mortgage rates. If mortgage rates can come down under 7 percent, we’ll see whether we see more buyer traffic.”

However, Sturtevant is less bullish on mortgage rates, noting that rate shifts don’t guarantee buyers the affordability break they seek. The Bright MLS economist pointed to the fact that home prices have continued rising in many markets, despite rates exceeding 7 percent.

“There is little reason to expect rates to come down further this year,” she said. “In fact, given this week’s inflation report, it is much more likely for us to see rates increase instead of decrease. Data on new pending contracts, showing activity and buyer traffic suggest that sales are going to continue to be anemic in the 4th quarter. It is very likely we will end 2026 with a total of fewer than 4 million existing home sales for the first time since the 1990s.”

#5469. The Generational Housing Divide: Millennials Had It Better Than Baby Boomers–Until the Pandemic Changed the Math

If millennials hadn’t spent so much money on avocado toast, they’d all own their dream home by now–right? Wrong. Just over half of millennials own their home. For the rest, housing costs have soared so much in recent years that skipping the avocado toast in their 20s wouldn’t have made a dent.

The story isn’t about constant struggle, though–it’s about timing. Elder millennials who bought a home in their early 30s had it better than baby boomers did at the same age: Historically low mortgage rates and higher household incomes meant those millennials spent about 27% of their income on housing at age 30, compared with 36% for boomers. Then the pandemic changed the math. Mortgage rates jumped from around 3% to nearly 7%, and home prices surged. Since rates rose above 6% in 2022, elder millennials have spent up to 35% of their income on monthly mortgage payments, compared with roughly 25% for boomers at the same age–even though millennials earn more, adjusted for inflation.

Boomers might point out that mortgage rates were much higher in their day. They’d be right: Rates peaked at over 16% in 1981 and stayed in double digits for much of the decade. But prices were lower. In the 1980s, when many boomers were in their 30s, the typical U.S. home sold for about $235,000 to $265,000 in today’s dollars. When elder millennials reached the same age–prime homebuying age–in the 2010s and 2020s, typical prices ranged from about $275,000 to $455,000.

Key takeaway: Buying at the wrong time was painful for both generations, but boomers had a better chance to recover. Falling rates throughout the late 1980s, 1990s and early 2000s gave them many opportunities to refinance into lower payments. Millennials who bought before 2022 secured historically low mortgages; those who bought later—or never managed to buy—face a much less forgiving market. Of course, it’s possible the market could become more forgiving for millennials over time; rates may eventually fall significantly enough that many millennials have the opportunity to refinance into lower payments.

This is based on an analysis of Redfin and U.S. Census data. A few notes to help contextualize the numbers: All dollar figures are adjusted for inflation. Much of the data illustrates each generation’s typical experience at a given age, combining everyone in that generation who has reached that age, whenever that happened for them. Because millennials are still aging into their 40s, for example, our 40-to-44 figures only capture the oldest millennials, who hit those ages between 2021 and 2025. All boomers have been through that age range, so their figures include the whole generation. Please see the end of this report for a detailed methodology.

In their early 30s, elder millennials who bought a home spent a smaller share of their income on housing than boomers did at the same age, despite much higher home prices. Imagine a median-earning millennial born in 1984 who bought a home at age 30. They would have spent around 27% of their income to purchase the typical home, within the “don’t spend more than 30% of your income on housing costs” rule of thumb.

Two factors helped: cheap borrowing and higher household incomes. Millennials benefited from roughly a decade of historically low mortgage rates; they fell below 3% in 2021. Millennials also tend to have higher household incomes than boomers did at the same age. At age 37, the typical elder millennial household earned an average of $100,000, compared with $88,000 when boomers were that age. The discrepancy is partly because two-income households are more common today. About 78% of women participate in the U.S. workforce, up from roughly 60% in 1980. It’s also worth noting that millennials typically work similar hours for more money than baby boomers at the same life stage.

The millennial advantage didn’t last. Mortgage rates jumped from around 3% in late 2021 to nearly 7% in late 2022, after home prices had surged about 40% nationwide during the pandemic homebuying frenzy. Rising rates often cool prices, but this time, prices didn’t fall. That mix of high prices and mortgage rates that had doubled from their pandemic-era low meant Americans had to spend a much higher share of their income to buy a home. Imagine that same millennial, born in 1984: If they bought a home at age 40 instead of 30, their housing costs shot up to about 35% of their income.

Rising prices and rates also priced many Americans completely out of the housing market, which is why elder millennials have a lower homeownership rate than baby boomers at the same age.

“For millennials who haven’t yet bought a home, affordability is a challenge. But it’s important to remember that you’re not trying to climb Mount Everest, you’re just trying to get back to 2018 or 2019, which was the last time the average homebuyer was spending just about 30% of their income on housing,” said Chen Zhao, Redfin’s head of economic research. “Before the pandemic, younger generations actually had it easier than the ones before them. But then home prices surged during the pandemic homebuying frenzy and mortgage rates shot up, while incomes kept growing at a normal pace–and the advantage flipped. If you bought in 2020 or 2021, you’re coming out ahead, but those years were the exception, not the rule. One piece of hope for younger Americans who haven’t yet bought a home: Home prices are already falling in parts of the U.S. and they’re softening in others, which means we could be headed back to 2018 or 2019 levels sooner rather than later.”

Millennials are also contending with other major expenses; childcare costs are squeezing them particularly hard. A recent Redfin analysis found that housing and childcare consume more than half of the typical American’s household income. Student loans are another big expense; millennials have significantly more student loan debt than boomers did at the same age.

Adult Gen Zers, who are in their twenties, are tracking behind millennials at the same stage of life. Gen Zers have spent anywhere from 40% of 60% of their income to buy the typical home since they’ve reached homebuying age. That’s partly because they’re still young enough that they haven’t yet hit their earnings peak, so their current income is lower than older generations, and partly because housing costs are higher than in the past. But as Gen Zers move through their careers, their earnings are likely to grow substantially, as they have for every generation before them. Combined with a gradual normalization in housing costs, homeownership should become increasingly attainable over time.

Baby boomers faced their own affordability crisis when they were young, in the 1980s. In their early 20s, the typical boomer household who bought a home would have spent more than 60% of its income on housing costs, reflecting the era’s runaway inflation and double-digit mortgage rates.

But their housing burden fell quickly as they aged, dropping to around 40% of income by their late 20s and 26% by their late 30s. Baby boomers’ homeownership rate steadily rose from about half in 1985 to over 70% by the late 1990s, and it kept climbing after that. By their 40s and 50s, the share of homebuyers’ income spent on housing had settled into the low-to-mid 20% range, lower than millennials at the same point in their life.

Much of that relief came from the same force that had hurt them initially—mortgage rates—as rates gradually declined through the 1980s and 1990s, letting many boomers refinance into far more manageable payments even as home prices kept climbing.

Millennials haven’t had the same opportunity. Those who bought before 2022 locked in historically low rates, while those who bought later faced a costly combination of high prices and climbing rates. Would-be buyers who couldn’t afford that combination were left out altogether.

“The housing market has historically been better for baby boomers than younger generations because lower home prices and higher rates are preferable to higher home prices and lower rates,” Zhao said. “You can refinance your rate into a lower housing payment, and that’s exactly what boomers did: They refinanced for up to 40 years as rates kept falling. Then home prices soared, which is why a lot of boomers are rich in real estate.”

That dynamic shows up clearly when you ask people directly. In a recent Redfin survey, more than three-quarters (76%) of baby boomers homeowners said they can easily afford their payment, while the rest struggle. Roughly half (53%) of millennial homeowners can easily afford their payment, and the other half struggle.

The same generational squeeze shows up in the reasons people are staying put in their current home. Among people unlikely to move soon, 43% of millennials cited high home prices as a reason, compared with 31% of boomers. Three in 10 (30%) millennials pointed to high mortgage rates, versus just 18% of boomers, likely because many baby boomers have paid off their mortgage and built up substantial equity. This is from a Redfin survey conducted by Ipsos in May 2026, fielded to 4,000 U.S. residents.

Consider two hypothetical couples. Alex and Jordan are millennials born in 1984 and live on two incomes, a common setup for millennial households. Pat and Chris are baby boomers born in 1956 and got by on one, more typical for their generation. The numbers below show what it would have cost each couple to buy a home to buy a home in their early 30s and their late 30s.

This analysis uses income data from 1976 to 2025 from the U.S. Census Bureau’s Current Population Survey Annual Social and Economic Supplement (CPS ASEC), accessed through IPUMS. The sample includes household heads aged 19 and older, and results are weighted using CPS household weights.

Each household is assigned to a generation based on the age of the household head in the survey year.

Home prices. We start with the 2025 median sale price of U.S. single-family homes from Redfin data ($456,409). Prices for earlier years are estimated by scaling that 2025 price back using the S&P Cotality Case-Shiller U.S. National Home Price Index from 1987 onward and the FHFA All-Transactions House Price Index for years before 1987. Both indexes are averaged by year.

Monthly housing payment. For each year, we calculate the monthly payment to buy a median-priced home. It covers principal, interest, property taxes and homeowners insurance. We assume:

Income and inflation. Household income is total household income as reported in the CPS ASEC. All income and payment figures are converted to 2025 dollars using the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U).

Share of income spent on housing. For each generation and age, we calculate the median monthly housing payment and the median household income, and divide the payment by one-twelfth of the income.

How to read the results by age.  Much of the data in this report shows each generation’s typical experience at a given age. Because a generation spans many birth years, people born at the start of that generation turn, say, 40 in a different calendar year than people born at the end of it. For this analysis, each age point combines averages for everyone from that generation who has reached that age, in whatever year that actually was for them. For instance, millennials (born 1981 to 1996) have only had the oldest members of their generation—those born in the early-to-mid 1980s—reach their 40s so far. So when we show what the typical 40-to-44-year-old millennial paid for housing, we’re only capturing people who hit that age between 2021 and 2025. Younger millennials haven’t gotten there yet. Baby boomers (born 1946 to 1964) are fully through that age range, their 40-to-44 data point include averages from all boomers.

As a data journalist at Redfin, Dana Anderson writes about the numbers behind real estate trends. Yingqi is a Senior Economist at Redfin. He studies housing market trends and explains what’s driving them for a broad audience. #5468. Why the Northeast Could Lead a Factory-Built Housing Boom

Most Americans picture sun-drenched mobile home parks across the South and Southeast when they think of manufactured housing, but more manufactured housing may soon start popping up across the Northeast and West.

A new economic research report from Realtor.com® senior economist Joel Berner takes an in-depth look at the manufactured housing guidelines in the 21st Century Road to Housing Act, which became law in June.

Berner found that cities across the Northeast—including Hartford, CT, Allentown, PA, and Albany, NY—have ideal conditions for a manufactured housing boom: “affordable land, unaffordable traditional new construction, and a low share of single-family starter home inventory.”If you’re not quite sure about what “manufactured housing" means, you’re not alone. For years, people seemingly used “mobile home” and “manufactured housing” interchangeably. But they’re not the same thing.

For one, the “mobile home” classification was retired in 1980, though many still use it colloquially. That year, it was replaced by the term “manufactured home.” Broadly, manufactured homes are those built in a factory and then transported to a site.

For years, federal Housing and Urban Development code required that all manufactured homes have a permanent steel towing frame underneath. New provisions in the Road to Housing Act, meant to spur more affordable housing, eliminated that requirement.

The act further entitles these new chassis-free homes to the same financing, titling, insurance, taxes, transport, and installation as conventional homes.

The hope is that creating this new category of manufactured home will help blunt one of the housing industry’s sharpest pain points: affordable starter homes.

Since the COVID-19 pandemic, the number of affordable starter homes for sale has markedly decreased.

Realtor.com research found roughly 300,000 fewer affordable “starter” listings on the market today than before the pandemic. The cost of those starter homes rose from $256,000 in 2019 to $344,000 in 2026. By comparison, the median price of a manufactured home in April 2026 was $134,800.

To understand what metros might see the biggest impact from this new type of manufactured home, Realtor.com scored the 100 largest metro areas on three metrics: the percentage of single-family starter homes (defined as listings priced at or below 80% of the local median) in the area; the relative price-per-square-foot premiums for traditional new construction; and the availability of affordable vacant land.

Six of the 10 opportunity metros were in the Northeast, including Hartford; Allentown; Albany; Rochester, NY; Syracuse, NY; and Worcester, MA. Other metros that made the list were Denver; Colorado Springs, CO; Albuquerque, NM; and Spokane, WA.

In Hartford, which ranked first, starter homes account for just 17.9% of single-family inventory, while site-built new construction costs 29.1% more per square foot than existing homes.

In third-ranked Allentown, single-family starter homes made up 22.9% of housing in the area, but new-construction costs were 33.6% more than existing homes. In sixth-ranked Albany, starter homes comprised 31.6% of the single-family inventory, but the price per square foot for new construction is 47% higher than for existing homes.

That’s nothing compared with seventh-ranked Rochester, where 33.7% of homes are starter but site-built new construction costs 97% more per square foot than existing homes.

While the economics in these cities are compelling, another reason manufactured housing may become more popular in these metros is that frigid Northeastern winters limit conventional housing construction. Meanwhile, manufactured housing can be assembled year-round.

Before Hartford, Albany, or any other metro can begin taking advantage of the Road to Housing Act’s new manufactured housing rules, municipal zoning laws will need to change, Berner found.

According to Land Use Labs data cited in the report, only about 17% of zoned land nationwide explicitly permits manufactured housing communities, and many municipalities enforce minimum floor-size rules or design restrictions that block factory-built units.

Julie Gerstein is a writer and editor based in Philadelphia. She previously worked at Business Insider as an executive editor covering news, entertainment, and digital culture, and was the company's founding Singapore bureau chief. She was also a senior editor at BuzzFeed, covering lifestyle, fashion, and beauty. She earned a B.A. in women's studies from the University of Pennsylvania and an M.A. in media and cultural studies from the University of Sussex.

#5467. Cloudera launches digital sovereignty platform spanning AI and infrastructure

Cloudera Inc. today announced a digital sovereignty package that it said enables organizations to maintain control over their data, artificial intelligence models and computing infrastructure regardless of where workloads run.

Cloudera for Digital Sovereignty combines the company’s Anywhere Cloud, Open Data Lakehouse and Unified Data Fabric technologies with open-weight AI models and model customization tools from Mistral SAS, with whom Cloudera recently partnered. The integrated offering supports deployment across sovereign clouds, private data centers and fully air-gapped environments that have no connection to external networks.

“As AI becomes more autonomous and embedded in critical operations, enterprises need to know that their data, models, and infrastructure can remain under their control even as technology and regulatory requirements change,” Cloudera Chief Technology Officer Sergio Gago said in a statement.

The offering provides consistent zero-trust access controls, data lineage tracking and governance policies across deployment environments. Those capabilities are intended to help organizations address requirements imposed by the European Union’s AI Act, Digital Operational Resilience Act and Network and Information Security Directive, among other regulations.

Governance policies also extend to the enterprise data that AI agents retrieve and use in performing tasks. Mistral’s open-weight models can run alongside governed data, enabling organizations to customize models locally and execute agentic workflows without exposing sensitive information.

Cloudera’s modular hybrid cloud architecture enables users to shift computing workloads between infrastructure providers and private data centers without rewriting applications or migrating or duplicating underlying data. Organizations can also selectively apply sovereignty controls to sensitive workloads without imposing the same restrictions across their entire computing estate.

Moor Insights & Strategy Inc. Chief Analyst Patrick Moorhead said AI has raised the bar on data protection. “A company can meet every line of its sovereignty policy and still not control who accesses its data or who can turn off the models it depends on,” he said in a statement.

Cloudera said it will supplement its Mistral partnership with an ecosystem of sovereign cloud providers and implementation partners. The company is initially targeting Europe but plans to expand the partner network into other regions and regulatory jurisdictions.

#5466. This Week Brings a Chance for Clarity After Mortgage Rates Rise on Hot Inflation and Hawkish Fed Remarks

Last Week’s Highlights: No shortage of big news last week, but for mortgage rates, what mattered the most was bad inflation data coupled with a Fed that turned sharply hawkish again. Last week’s inflation data came in higher than expected and the most worrisome part was that the drivers were broad-based. It looks like core PCE, the Fed’s preferred measure of inflation, is set to come in around 0.3% month-over-month this year, or 3.2% year-over-year, which would mean that it’s moving in the wrong direction relative to the Fed’s target.

The Fed also released its meeting calendar for 2027. It will hold the usual 8 meetings, but the October 2027 meeting will be a strategy meeting where they will not change rates. As a result, they’re moving the December 2027 meeting to November. Even though this means 9 weeks instead of the usual 6 between policy meetings at the end of 2027, this should have minimal effect on monetary policy.

Finally, NAR reported existing home sales at an annualized rate of 3.75 million in October. That’s the lowest rate since August 2010 and lower than any month these last four years. This is consistent with Redfin data showing a historically low level of housing demand.

Upcoming Attractions: The biggest piece of economic data this week is the Tuesday retail sales report, which will give another look at how consumers are faring, but is unlikely to move rates much.

Investors will also get a chance to dissect the minutes from the last Fed meeting on Wednesday. And we will hear from other key FOMC members throughout the week. The ones to watch are New York Fed President Williams today, tomorrow, and Wednesday; Fed Chair Warsh today; Cleveland Fed President Hammack today, tomorrow, and Thursday; and Fed Governor Waller tomorrow.

Chen Zhao is the head of economics research, where she produces research on the housing market for public and internal audiences. Previously, she was an executive director leading housing finance and financial markets research at the JPMorgan Chase Institute. Prior to joining JPMCI, Chen was an economics consultant at Analysis Group, Inc., where she worked on financial litigation cases and led teams conducting health economics and outcomes research on behalf of pharmaceutical companies. While in graduate school, Chen was with the Center for Economic Studies and the Social Economic and Housing Statistics Division at the US Census Bureau, where she conducted applied microeconomics research using large scale restricted-access linked survey-administrative data. She started her career at the White House Council of Economic Advisers, where she focused on labor and health economics.

#5465. He sold Bibles door to door. Now he runs a 35,000-home luxury exchange club in 103 countries

What do door-to-door Bible salesmen have to do with luxury real estate? For Wade Shealy, everything.

On this episode of Real Estate Insiders Unfiltered, James Dwiggins and Keith Robinson sit down with Shealy, founder and CEO of ThirdHome, the luxury home exchange club he started in 2010 with just two homes. Today it has more than 35,000 homes in over 100 countries. Shealy shares how selling Bibles and dictionaries door to door paid his way through the University of Georgia and how it led him to Hilton Head in 1984 to a career in resort real estate.

He explains why second homeowners kept coming back within five years wanting to sell and how that pattern became the idea for ThirdHome. He also walks through how he signed up his first 1,500 members and how the club’s key system works. Plus, he shares the biggest lesson he’s learned from his partner, Mrs. Fields founder Debbi Fields: Make everyone you meet feel important.

They also get into handling rejection, taking big risks and why Shealy believes very few people will buy a vacation home without a home exchange membership 10 years from now.

Shealy explains the luxury home exchange club model simply. Owners deposit unused weeks in their second home and earn credits called keys. They use those keys to book stays in other members’ homes, paying only an exchange fee of around $900 instead of thousands in rent. The club has now completed 100,000 exchanges, and Shealy says many members who would never rent out their home happily exchange it.

For agents, Shealy points to ThirdHome’s ambassador program. In Cabo San Lucas, developers began offering ThirdHome access as part of their sales pitch, and the club grew to roughly 8,000 properties there. He believes the next generation of buyers will expect mobility and experiences, not just a single vacation home.

His advice for agents: Look at what everyone else is doing, and do the opposite. Above all, keep changing, because if you’re marketing the same way you did 20 years ago, you’re already behind.

#5464. Industrial internet of things satellite platform Myriota raises $40M to scale its constellation and expand

Australia-based Myriota Pty. Ltd., a global satellite platform for the industrial internet of things, today announced it has raised $40 million in the first portion of its Series C to launch next-generation satellites and accelerate customer adoption across international markets.

Main Sequence Ventures, Hostplus and Australia’s National Reconstruction Fund Corporation co-led the round. Funds SA joined as a new investor. The round raised the company’s total funding to more than $107.5 million, and is expected to close in early 2027.

Founded in 2015, Myriota’s platform makes satellite connectivity commercially viable for large-scale industrial IoT, using the same core technology to track mining equipment and trailers to also monitor fuel tanks, livestock water supplies and off-grid solar.

The company’s platform combines satellite connectivity, low-power devices, field installation tools and fleet management software to support existing infrastructure. The objective is to provide access to communication tools that connect what is in place with turnkey service, so a company can connect devices, machines and smart sensors no matter how remote they are.

“We’re at the beginning of a fundamental shift in industrial IoT,” Chief Executive Ben Cade said. “Industries increasingly rely on data from the field to make decisions about their operations, assets and resources, and as AI moves into the physical world, that data becomes even more essential.”

The company expanded its platform over the past 12 months with the launch of HyperPulse, a global 5G non-terrestrial network, or NTN, and terrestrial service, and AssetHawk, a rugged, long-life asset tracker designed to make it economical to track industrial objects.

Alongside the expansion, it also grew into new verticals such as industrial fuels. It monitors and tracks fuel deployments across North America and Latin America, with EMEA and Asia Pacific to follow.

Myriota competes in a sector led by established operators such as Iridium Communications Inc., Orbcomm Inc. and Viasat Inc., alongside a growing field of providers pursuing cheaper, standards-based connections for industrial sensors and trackers.

The company said it intends to use the funds to expand its space infrastructure, including developing and launching its next-generation satellites.

#5463. Inside 4 Jaw-Dropping New York Homes With Front-Row Views of the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade

This Thanksgiving marks the 100th anniversary of the annual Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade, and while the weather forced the parade to be postponed for the first time in its history, thousands are still expected to cram the streets of Manhattan to watch the iconic event on its rescheduled date, Saturday.

But imagine having a front-row seat without ever leaving home?

There are plenty of apartments, condos, and penthouses that line the parade route that runs along Central Park, and we found four active listings that would allow you to watch the parade year after year without ever stepping outside.

Why it’s here: Residence 7C sits along Central Park West on West 75th Street, putting the parade right outside its windows.

“With over 45 feet of frontage along the parade route, balloons floating right past the windows, and sweeping southeast views, it's the ultimate vantage point for the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade,” explained listing agent Jessica Svensson of Douglas Elliman.

The 3,000-square-foot unit is distinguished by its grand prewar proportions, including a nearly 30-foot great room, a 21-foot formal dining room, and 10-foot ceilings.

Its gracious floor plan separates the entertaining spaces from the private bedroom wing, while the corner positioning offers sweeping views east across Central Park and south toward the Manhattan skyline and Billionaires' Row.

Other noteworthy features include a primary suite with western exposure, a flexible library or home office, an eat-in kitchen, central AC, a built-in bar with refrigeration, and a separate laundry room.

Jessica Svensson of Douglas Elliman is the listing agent.

Why it’s here: Thanks to the building’s 1931 column-free corner design, Units 5Q and 4P offer unobstructed northern views up Central Park West, ideal for watching the Thanksgiving Day Parade.

“For years three generations have gathered to watch the parade in this special home,” said listing agent Nealy Nusbaum Erber of Christie's International Real Estate New York.

Standout building amenities include a state-of-the-art fitness center, golf simulator, Pilates room, children’s playroom, residents’ lounge, private work suites, and a pet washing station.

Nealy Nusbaum Erber of Christie's International Real Estate New York is the listing agent.

Why it’s here: Unit 7EG offers prime parade-watching views from three of its front rooms.

“The unit is on the 7th floor, the perfect height to view the passing balloons. It has huge picture windows where you can view and photograph the parade, crowds, and balloons.  My husband, an amateur yet published photographer, has shot pictures of the parade on many occasions from those front windows,” explained listing agent Barbara Fox of Brown Harris.

This unique combination of two apartments comprises approximately 4,000 square feet in a top Central Park West building. Located between 65th and 66th Streets in the bustling Lincoln Center neighborhood, there’s no shortage of fine dining, gourmet food shops, wonderful shopping, and the serenity of Central Park just across the street

Barbara Fox of Brown Harris Stevens is the listing agent.

Why it’s here: Watching the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade from 15 Central Park West feels like having a private viewing box above one of New York City's most beloved traditions.

“Complete with beautiful finishes and fixtures across 3,364 square feet plus an additional suite for guests or staff and a wine cellar, this home also provides access to the unparalleled services and amenities that have made Robert A.M. Stern’s 15 Central Park West is one of New York City's most prestigious addresses,” said listing agent Cathy Franklin of Corcoran East Side.

The location is also remarkable. Situated along Central Park West, you can enjoy direct access to iconic Central Park while being moments from Lincoln Center, and some of the city's finest restaurants, shopping, and cultural institutions.

“It's a neighborhood that provides a great mix of tranquility and energy, which is why it continues to attract discerning buyers from around the world,” added Franklin.

Cathy Franklin of Corcoran East Side is the listing agent.

#5462. The rise of the multi-market agent: Why local expertise is going global

Wealth is mobile, and so are luxury clients. Here’s how the multi-market real estate agent combines local expertise with a connected brokerage network.

Ask a luxury client where they live, and the answer is increasingly more than one place. A primary home in Los Angeles, a ski house in Aspen, a pied-à-terre in New York, a winter retreat in Miami or the Caribbean.

Wealth has become more mobile, and so have the people who hold it. The agents who serve these clients best are evolving alongside them, building expertise across markets and cultivating relationships that extend well beyond their own backyards.

That shift is changing what it means to be a local expert. For brokerage leaders, it also raises an important question: Are we building networks that reflect how our clients actually live?

Remote work, flexible schedules and a generation of buyers who think of themselves as global citizens have loosened the link between where someone earns, where they live and where they invest.

Today’s luxury buyers are driven by lifestyle, whether that means access to mountains, water, a particular school system or a city’s cultural calendar, and they are comfortable buying in places where they spend only part of the year. What has not changed is their expectation of personalized service.

For these clients, a traditional handoff creates friction. Each time they are passed from one agent to another, they repeat their goals, rebuild trust and wonder whether anyone sees the full picture. A client’s real estate portfolio is one story. Their advisor should be able to tell it across markets.

Going global does not mean going generic. A Manhattan co-op board, a Florida insurance requirement, a Colorado water right and a California disclosure obligation each carry real consequences, and clients need professionals who understand the market in which they are buying or selling.

The mistake is confusing geographic reach with geographic expertise. The strongest multi-market agents know where their knowledge is deepest and where collaboration adds value. The future of the multi-market real estate agent isn’t about being an expert everywhere. It’s about knowing where your expertise ends, who to bring into the conversation and how to make that collaboration seamless for the client.

When a client has a positive experience with an agent in one city, that relationship shouldn’t end at the city limits. But there is a meaningful difference between providing a referral and extending a trusted relationship. If an agent simply passes along a name, the client starts over. If that introduction comes with shared context and a clear understanding of the client’s priorities, the experience feels seamless.

Trust is portable, but only when it is supported by consistent service and relationships built before a client needs them.

A global footprint alone does not create a global client experience. Offices in multiple markets mean little if they operate independently. Brokerages need to provide the infrastructure that makes cross-market relationships work, including introductions between offices, shared market intelligence, consistent training and clear expectations around communication and referrals.

At The Agency, we encourage agents to bring colleagues from other offices into client relationships early, so clients experience a connected team rather than a series of separate introductions. Technology helps agents share insights, access inventory and present properties remotely, but the real advantage comes from the relationships behind it.

Start by looking at the markets that consistently appear in your referral activity and client conversations. Those patterns show where to build stronger partnerships between offices.

Invest in cross-market education so agents recognize regional nuances and regulatory considerations and know when to bring in specialized expertise. Set clear collaboration standards for how clients are introduced, who takes the lead and how agents stay involved. Then measure success beyond the transaction: Did the client feel supported, and was communication consistent?

As brokerage leaders, we should be asking whether our networks are simply growing in size or becoming more connected. Those are very different measures of success.

Local expertise has never been more valuable. What is changing is its reach. The brokerages that treat their agents’ knowledge as a connected network, rather than a set of separate territories, will be better positioned to serve today’s clients and the next generation of buyers who increasingly see the world, not one city, as their real estate market.

Rainy Hake Austin is president of The Agency in Los Angeles. Get connected on Instagram.

#5460. Key insights from HPE’s Q4 earnings report

ANALYSIS by Zeus Kerravala

Hewlett Packard Enterprise Co.delivered a record fiscal fourth quarter this week, roughly doubling its fiscal 2027 growth outlook, but its stock gave back nearly all of the prior day’s rally. The selloff suggests Wall Street still prices HPE as a low-margin server vendor, even though the results describe a networking and artificial intelligence infrastructure company with demand exceeding its ability to ship.

Fourth-quarter revenue rose 50%, to $14.5 billion, orders grew 88%, and adjusted earnings of $1.43 per share topped the high end of guidance. HPE now expects fiscal 2027 revenue to grow 27% to 35%, with adjusted earnings of $5.05 to $5.35 per share, according to its earnings release.

I joined a briefing with Chief Executive Antonio Neri and a small group of independent analysts shortly before the results came out. Here are my four takeaways for investors and information technology leaders:

Neri explained that networking orders grew more than 4.5 times faster than networking revenue in the quarter, up from 3.5 times the quarter before, and HPE exited the year with $10.5 billion in AI backlog.

HPE doubled its networking purchase commitments over the summer and raised them again in the fourth quarter, but those components carry lead times of 28 to 40-plus weeks, so Neri expects networking conversion to pick up starting in the second quarter. Supply constraints are a better problem to have than weak demand, but they mean fiscal 2027 hinges on converting orders rather than winning them.

The Juniper Networks integration is complete, and the annual cost-synergy target has risen to $800 million, but the bigger story remains the profit mix. Chief Financial Officer Marie Myers said networking will account for more than 40% of HPE’s operating profit by the fourth quarter of fiscal 2027, up from less than a quarter of revenue. AI is a major driver, with routing orders growing by triple digits as customers connect AI data centers to one another.

Security was the soft spot, which Neri called “just timing.” When I asked whether the security portfolio is where he wants it as the industry consolidates around big platforms, he argued for a different path.

“Fortinet and we have a different strategy — the convergence of security and networking — and we are taking it all the way down to the silicon level,” he said. The convergence of networking and security is underway but will take time to execute, as a considerable amount of technical debt must go through its depreciation cycle. In a greenfield situation, organizations can easily deploy a converged solution, but in a brownfield environment, it requires much more work. This is the right strategy, but it remains a “prove-it” business for HPE.

Many neoclouds rely on vendor financing and chip-backed debt, raising real concerns about who is left exposed if the buildout slows. HPE says it has stayed out, and Neri was quite emphatic about it on the briefing.

“I want to be clear: We have not financed any neocloud through HPFS, our financing arm,” he said. “We have zero exposure to any AI financing for neocloud.” HPE has likely left some revenue on the table, but it drew the line in the right place. It will sell to neoclouds, as its $1.2 billion Vultr order shows, without acting as their bank. Enterprise and sovereign customers account for the majority of its cumulative AI orders, and if the neocloud financing chain breaks, HPE’s financing arm won’t be the one holding the paper.

Training built the first phase of AI infrastructure, and Neri believes inference will build the next and will dominate demand for AI infrastructure. “I believe by the end of the decade, 80% will be in AI inferencing,” he said. “Much of that will land on-prem. Much of that will be distributed, for sure. That’s why the server business is structurally well-positioned.”

Once agents are in production, token costs become a recurring bill, and companies will want inference running alongside their own data. Those servers require far more memory and pull in storage and services, which is better business than racking graphics processing units for a hyperscaler.

Evidence of this is the interest in Helios, the Advanced Microdevices Inc. rack that uses HPE’s Ethernet switching rather than Nvidia’s proprietary interconnect. I asked Neri whether Jensen Huang’s brief departure from Nvidia Corp. had opened that door. He said interest was building before then, as customers look to diversify.

HPE shares jumped 17% on Monday ahead of the report as part of a broader AI rally, then fell about 13% in early trading on Tuesday, ending near where they started the week. I see three reasons for this.

The first is margins. Cloud & AI operating margin was 18.4% in the quarter, and HPE guided to about 14% for fiscal 2027. Reuters reported that JPMorgan analysts called margin mix the key debate for investors.

The second is pricing. Myers said higher selling prices have been the biggest driver of server growth, and she expects gross margin to moderate in the second half as AI server volumes ramp and costs rise faster than pricing.

The third is timing. HPE expects about 54% of revenue in the second half, with the ramp tied to Helios shipments, the Oracle Corp. deal, customer data center readiness and component supply. Those are fair execution questions, but they miss the shift in where HPE’s profit comes from.

On the topic of margins, the 18.4% came off an unusual stretch of favorable pricing that should not have been modeled as permanent. Neri argued the guide is still “significantly higher than any historical margin we have had in this business,” and he’s right outside the past year. A year ago, the segment’s margin was 9.3%. Margin rate also isn’t margin dollars. At 30% to 40% revenue growth, my math shows Cloud & AI adding well over $1 billion in operating profit at the midpoint.

The bears are right that price-driven server growth doesn’t warrant a premium multiple, which is why the mix matters more. The market is fixated on the segment whose margins are normalizing and ignoring the one whose margins are expanding. Adjusted earnings per share are still guided to grow by 27% to 35%, in line with revenue growth. That’s far from the margin doom-and-gloom narrative on the stock.

The back-half concern is real but manageable. Myers described the pipeline as multiples of the backlog, and Neri said the guide assumes only historical win rates against it.

Then there’s quality. HPE is guiding to about 30% growth and at least $5.5 billion in free cash flow, has no neocloud financing exposure and has already brought leverage below its target. It trades at about eight times the midpoint of its adjusted earnings guidance. “I don’t see us at a multiple that is 8 to 9x; it makes no sense whatsoever,” Neri said on the earnings call.

For old HPE, that’s true, as it’s a server vendor, but HPE is increasingly a network vendor each quarter. In fact, during our pre-call with Neri, he led with networking and spoke at length about the business before pivoting to the server business. Expect networking to continue to drive a larger share of profits.

Fiscal 2027 is an execution year. HPE must convert purchase commitments into shipments, ramp Helios and prove that networking margins can climb even as cloud and AI margins settle. I’ll be watching networking order conversion more closely than server margins. If HPE executes, today’s multiple will prove to be too low.

Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

#5459. Mortgage Rates Dip Ahead of Holiday, Application Activity Increases as Rates Fluctuate

Real estate housing market decline concept. Wooden house model standing next to falling red arrow on floor with window blind shadows. Decreasing property value and mortgage rate.

Even while lingering above 7%, slight dips in the average mortgage rate were enough to spur home-buyer activity this past week.

The latest Market Composite Index from the Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA)—its measure of mortgage loan activity volume and includes purchases and refinances—shows mortgage application activity increasing 6.1% on a seasonally adjusted basis, a notable increase from last week’s 2.3% decrease. On an unadjusted basis, the Index increased 3% compared to a 5% decrease the previous week.

This week’s increase follows weeks of fluctuations as the 30-year fixed mortgage rate still remains over 7%–this past week decreasing to 7.21% from 7.28% the previous week, according to Freddie Mac and currently sits at 7.29%, according to Mortgage News Daily.

“Mortgage rates moved higher, with the 30-year fixed rate rising to 7.28 percent (last week),” said Joel Kan, CMB, MBA’s vice president and deputy chief economist. “While mortgage rates increased slightly on a weekly average basis, rates declined over the course of the week, which likely spurred purchase application activity.”

“Purchase applications reached their strongest weekly pace since September but remained well behind last year’s pace,” he added.

The latest Freddie Mac Primary Mortgage Market Survey® released Wednesday ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday, also shows the 30-year FRM is still up year-over-year more than a full percentage point from 6.23% last year. The 15-year FRM averaged 6.66%, up from last week’s 6.45%. A year ago at this time, the 15-year FRM averaged 5.51%.

“Mortgage rates currently are about a percentage point higher than a year ago, while home prices are also still rising in many local markets,” said Bright MLS Chief Economist Lisa Sturtevant. Affordability is the biggest constraint on housing market activity, and until affordability eases, the pace of home sales transactions is going to be far below average. Existing home sales are on pace to come in below 4 million for 2026, which will be the first time sales have tracked below that level since the mid-1990s.

“Inflation continues to exceed the Fed’s target raising expectations for a December Fed rate hike, placing a floor under interest rates, including mortgage rates,” said Realtor.com Chief Economist Danielle Hale. “Despite this week’s decline, mortgage rates remain roughly a percentage point above where they were at this point in 2025, adding another headwind for buyers contending with high home prices.”

Kan pointed to a rise in adjustable rate mortgages (ARMs) as most notable this week.

“A larger share of borrowers relied on ARM loans for lower monthly payments, which accounted for 11.5 percent of applications, the highest share in more than a year,” he said. “At 6.39 percent, the ARM mortgage rate was nearly a full percentage lower than the 30-year fixed rate last week.”
