#5404. FCC clears SpaceX to put up to 1 million Starmind data centers in space

Elon Musk’s Space Exploration Technologies Corp. today received approval from the U.S. Federal Communications Commission to deploy up to 1 million Starmind satellites designed to operate as data centers in orbit.

Issued by the FCC’s Space Bureau under delegated authority, the order is described by the agency as “the first authorization in U.S. history for a constellation of data centers in space.”

“By moving compute capacity beyond Earth, SpaceX and the many competitors working on their own orbital data centers are meeting the moment,” FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said. “This is the kind of American ingenuity that can unite our strengths in space and advanced technology, reinforce our economic leadership, and expand prosperity here at home.”

Replying to Carr on X, Musk wrote that Starmind “will be a great asset to America and the world.”

Under the terms of the approval, the Starmind satellites are to sit in six orbital shells, or altitude bands, between 500 and 1,002 kilometers, below the 2,000-kilometer ceiling in SpaceX’s original application. Most communications will run over optical links to other satellites, including those in the Starlink network. The license itself covers a backup Ka-band radio system for emergency telemetry, tracking and command.

The approval does come with conditions. SpaceX’s orbital debris plan was found to comply with the agency’s rules only for satellites below 600 kilometers, and four of the six shells sit above that line. Before deploying anything higher, SpaceX is required to file a modification application containing a final debris plan.

A request from the company to retire some of those higher satellites into disposal orbits around Earth or the sun, rather than having them re-enter the atmosphere within five years, was deferred for lack of information.

To keep the authorization, SpaceX has to have its first Starmind satellite in operation by Nov. 25, 2033. The schedule then calls for 100,000 satellites by 2035, 500,000 by 2038 and the full 1 million by 2040. Missing any of the deadlines would void the license.

Petitions to deny the application from Amazon.com Inc.’s Amazon Leo satellite business, Viasat Inc. and the American Astronomical Society were all rejected. In a March filing, Amazon had described the plan as “a lofty ambition rather than a real plan.”

According to the bureau, nothing in the FCC’s rules limits how many satellites a single constellation can include. Astronomers’ concerns about the satellites’ brightness in infrared were ruled to fall outside the scope of a radio license.

SpaceX first applied for the system in January, shortly before it acquired Musk’s artificial intelligence company xAI Corp. Orbital data centers then featured in SpaceX’s pitch to investors ahead of its record initial public offering in June. Built around a space-optimized version of Nvidia Corp.’s Vera Rubin NVL72 rack-scale system, the first-generation Starmind satellite, known as AI1, could reach orbit as early as the third quarter of next year, according to Musk.

The competitors Carr referred to include Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin LLC, which applied in March for Project Sunrise, a planned network of up to 51,600 data center satellites. Starcloud Inc., a startup developing AI data centers in orbit, raised $250 million at a $2.3 billion valuation in August.

#5403. Soneil Spark Launches Spark Cashback: A Home Charger, Free with a Refundable Deposit, That Pays You Back Every Time You Plug In

Launching in time for Spark Season, the Soneil group's holiday gift to EV drivers

BRAMPTON, ON, Nov. 26, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Soneil Spark, the EV charging business of Soneil Electronics, today publicly launched Spark Cashback, a program that turns the Clean Fuel credits your home charging creates into cash in your pocket. It launches alongside Spark Season, the Soneil group's way of giving back to EV drivers this holiday season.

"We've spent more than 30 years building power electronics people can rely on, and Spark Cashback puts that to work for everyday drivers," said Sonya Jain, CEO of Soneil Spark. "The charger is free with a deposit you get back, and every charge puts money back in your pocket. Spark Season is how we give back, with a gift that keeps giving and is even better shared with someone you care about."

Under Canada's Clean Fuel Regulations, fuel suppliers must buy compliance credits, and charging an EV at home creates them. Your Spark charger tracks each session over Wi-Fi, Soneil Spark sells the credits, and you get a share as cash by Interac e-Transfer. The fuel industry helps offset your everyday charging, while you keep driving without tailpipe emissions.

The charger is free with a refundable deposit. Once you reach 1,250 kWh, the full deposit comes back, earlier than most comparable free-charger programs. You end up with a home charger that cost you nothing, apart from shipping, plus cash back on top. How soon depends on your driving.

A program is easier to trust when you know who is behind it. Soneil Spark designs and builds a complete range of EV charging under one roof, including mobile charging trailers for fleets and enterprise, all on our own technology, made in Canada, rather than rebadged off-the-shelf hardware. Soneil Electronics has reliably supplied batteries and chargers globally across a wide range of industries and applications, from golf carts and cleaning appliances to material handling and emergency power. The company has supplied more than 5 million chargers, and every Soneil Spark charger is backed by 24/7 North American-based support.

Spark Season: the gift that keeps giving back

Most gifts get unwrapped once. This one keeps showing up in your bank account every time you charge. Spark Season is the Soneil group's way of giving back, with promos throughout the holiday season, so check back regularly. But don't wait: if a better promo comes along after you sign up, just ask and we'll readjust your offer.

Pay it forward, in the most literal sense. Don't just tell the EV drivers you care about, get it for them. Family, close friends, anyone who drives electric can have a charger that's free with a refundable deposit and pays them back, with the fuel industry's compliance credits doing the giving.

Open to new customers with a Canadian address and Wi-Fi at the charger. Quebec drivers can choose the Canada-wide offer or a Quebec-specific program. Getting it for family or a friend? They need to be a new customer at an eligible address. Sign up and see this season's deposit, rates, bonus and warranty terms at soneilspark.com/pages/spark-cashback.

Free charger requires a refundable deposit, plus shipping, refunded after 1,250 kWh of charging; timing depends on your driving. Promotional pricing and bonuses change throughout the season; readjustment on request, terms apply. The connection bonus is paid once, after the charger is connected and verified. Cash back is paid out at each payout milestone. Deposit and bonus amounts, rates, warranty terms and full terms are on the sign-up page. Comparisons are based on published terms of comparable free-charger deposit programs. Earnings are not guaranteed and are not income. New customers only.

Soneil Spark is the EV charging division of Soneil Electronics, a power electronics manufacturer with more than 30 years of experience, associated with Soneil Investments, a commercial property investment and asset management company with more than $2.2 billion AUM. It designs and builds Level 2 home and commercial chargers, DC fast charging up to 480 kW, the Mobile EV Charging Trailer and Mobile Battery Energy Storage, made in Canada and available across North America. Learn more at soneilspark.com.

#5400. US intelligence agencies reportedly brief Congress about Alice Huang

U.S. intelligence agencies reportedly briefed Congressional staffers about Alice Huang, the cloud executive at the center of the Jensen Huang controversy.

The classified discussion took place on Tuesday, sources told the New York Times and the Wall Street Journal today. It was attended by staff members of the House and Senate intelligence committees. The briefing is said to have included representatives of the FBI, CIA and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence.

Alice Huang is a former executive at Megaspeed, a Singaporean cloud provider that has reportedly bought billions of dollars worth of Nvidia Corp. chips. The company is under investigation for allegedly breaching U.S. export controls. Those controls prohibit companies from selling cutting-edge artificial intelligence chips to customers in China.

On Oct. 29, the Times revealed that Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang had an affair with Alice Huang. The paper stated that she had been “found to be passing intelligence” to China. A few days later, other outlets reported that U.S. officials had not yet concluded that Alice Huang is a spy. The U.S. Justice Department reaffirmed that’s the case shortly thereafter.

According to the Times, this week’s classified Congressional briefing included a summary of the information that U.S. intelligence agencies have collected about Alice Huang. Those agencies’ representatives reportedly “did not dispute” that she had gathered information for China. However, they stated that there’s no evidence China’s MSS spy agency directed her to initiate the affair.

Some U.S. officials reportedly believe Alice Huang can still be considered a spy. Others are said to see her ties to the country’s intelligence service as ”more circumstantial.” According to the Journal, officials don’t believe that Alice Huang passed any “intelligence of significance” to China.

The briefers reportedly told Congressional staffers that Kang Wei, a businessman believed to be Huang’s husband, is a “more significant” figure. They stated that Kang is a Chinese intelligence asset who was “often” in touch with the country’s spy agency.

On Nov. 12, the Journal reported that Kang had known Jensen Huang for over a decade. The publication later revealed that he had built a data center network in China.

The briefing reportedly did not cover the most sensitive information the U.S. intelligence community has gathered about Alice Huang. Additionally, it didn’t include a classified memo about her relationship with Jensen Huang that was drafted under the supervision of U.S. State Secretary Marco Rubio. Congressional staffers requested a copy of the memo.

Jensen Huang is set to appear before three House committees on Dec. 1. Prior to the spy controversy, he was reportedly scheduled to make a product announcement that day. The closed-door briefing will be followed by a public hearing before the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 3.

#5399. U.S. Treasury has an unusual national debt headache: An $18 billion hole from GLP-1s, with families spending $500 less a year on groceries

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent—and whoever comes after him at the end of Trump’s term—has an unusual new headache to consider when it comes to budget deficits. Investors are usually concerned with long-dated Treasuries pushing up interest rates, or international lenders choosing to put their cash into other assets. But in the era of GLP-1s, weight-loss medications are a new concern for the budget bottom line.Nearly 60 million people will be using GLP-1s such as Ozempic and Mounjaro by 2030, Oxford Economics suggested in a note shared with Fortune this week. This is well above other estimates published earlier this year. JP Morgan predicted in February that 25 million Americans would be using the medication by the end of the decade, for instance.

But demand has surprised in 2026, so much so that Denmark’s national bank increased its economic growth estimates in September, largely due to U.S. demand for Novo Nordisk products Ozempic and Wegovy.

But with the drugs now covered by government health programs and contributing to potentially longer lifespans, Oxford Economics’ Grace Zwemmer writes that GLP-1s “are an additional factor driving a deterioration in the fiscal situation over the next decade.”

Budget watchdogs like the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) have already said the fiscal impact of approving GLP-1s is going to be a problem for Medicare. In 2024, the CBO wrote that coverage of drugs for specific use cases would, on net, increase federal spending by about $35 billion between 2026 and 2034.

Zwemmer suggests the costs will be higher due to above-expected demand. More than 1.1 million beneficiaries in the U.S. have signed up for discounted GLP-1s under a pilot introduced this year, allowing patients to access the drugs for reasons other than Type-2 diabetes.

“On net, we estimate Medicare coverage of GLP-1s for weight loss will add close to $18 billion to the deficit by 2034. This is roughly 0.9% of the annual deficit, but a much smaller share of GDP, only about 5bps. The cumulative cost over 2026-2034 comes to around $107bn, about three times greater than the CBO’s estimate,” Zwemmer wrote

From a macroeconomic perspective, there are also benefits to the government in supporting access to these medications. Zwemmer says that up to 480,000 more Americans could be working by 2030 thanks to improved health. This would contribute a meaningful lift to payrolls and taxable incomes in a labor force shrinking due to aging and lower immigration.

Individual households that use GLP-1s could also see changes in their personal finances.

A 2024 study by Cornell and Numerator found that households with at least one GLP-1 user reduced their grocery spending by 5.3% within six months of adoption. Most categories saw spending declines, but the largest reductions were concentrated in calorie-dense, processed categories, including a 10.1% decline in savory snacks.

The change in consumer behavior is so marked that GLP-1s are helping “keep a lid on food inflation,” Oxford Economics added. Zwemmer writes: “We estimate that GLP-1-using households will reduce their annual spending on food both at home and away from home by a combined $500.”

Zwemmer also notes that some of those funds may be diverted into buying new wardrobes, highlighting that new starters on GLP-1s are likely to spend $200 on refreshing their clothes. The U.S. economist added: “Scaled up to our estimate of nearly 40 million users entering 2027, this would translate to an $8bn uplift in apparel spending next year.”

Eleanor Pringle is an award-winning senior reporter at Fortune covering news, the economy, and personal finance. Eleanor previously worked as a business correspondent and news editor in regional news in the U.K. She completed her journalism training with the Press Association after earning a degree from the University of East Anglia.

#5398. Elon Musk Is Building the Future We Saw in the Movies. So Who’s Imagining the Technology of Tomorrow?

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

A new generation of entrepreneurs is emerging, armed with tools that previous generations could only dream of.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Remember The Jetsons? Since the 1960s, humans have watched a world of flying cars, automated homes, and robotic assistants that seemed pure fantasy. Today, Elon Musk is working to bring elements of that future to life. And it isn’t just The Jetsons. The 2004 film I, Robot imagined humanoid robots and intelligent machines.

Twenty years later, when Tesla unveiled its Optimus robot, the film’s director, Alex Proyas, joked: “Can I have my designs back, please?”

That raises a bigger question: If engineers are building the technology we saw in yesterday’s movies, who’s imagining the technology of tomorrow?

Star Trek, for example, imagined communicators resembling mobile phones, voice-operated computers and medical scanning devices decades before they became everyday reality. These weren’t engineering blueprints; they were creative visions of what life might look like.

We celebrate the engineer, programmer and scientist who turn ideas into reality, but rarely the people who first imagined the possibility.

We have become obsessed with qualifications and specialization. We do need brilliant doctors, engineers and scientists, but mastering an existing discipline is not the same as imagining an entirely new one.

You can be an exceptional engineer or programmer and still struggle to imagine what the world will need in twenty years.

Innovation requires more than knowing how to build something. It requires the instinct, faith and foresight to recognize what is worth building in the first place.

The greatest entrepreneurs are not necessarily those who understand every component of the technology they are developing. They are the people who can see beyond it, understand what people will want and bring together the talent capable of turning that vision into reality.

Artificial intelligence is transforming the economics of production and making powerful tools accessible to individuals who previously needed entire teams, specialist equipment and substantial financial resources. Quantum computing promises another leap in processing capability.

However, having access to powerful tools doesn’t automatically make someone an innovator. As the old saying goes, “A fool with a tool is still a fool.”

When everyone has access to increasingly powerful technology, the real advantage belongs to those who know what to do with it, and, more importantly, can imagine what to do with it next.

The World Economic Forum’s Future of Jobs Report 2025 identified creative thinking among the most important skills for the future workforce. The future isn’t a competition between technical and creative people; it’s about bringing those capabilities together, with imagination providing direction.

The next generation of world-changing entrepreneurs may come from filmmaking, storytelling, design, music or architecture, imagining experiences and industries we haven’t yet thought to ask for.

As we become fascinated by artificial intelligence and intelligent machines, we risk overlooking what makes us extraordinary: instinct, imagination, emotional intelligence, empathy and our ability to create stories that move people.

A machine can analyze millions of films, identify patterns and generate technically impressive productions, but the human experience that gives a story its meaning comes from living, loving, losing, believing, questioning and understanding the world through our own eyes.

For me, creativity is not simply a professional skill; it is one of the most fundamental expressions of being human.

There is a philosophical and spiritual dimension to this too. For those of us who believe in a Creator, if humanity was made in the image of an intelligent Creator, perhaps our own ability to create is one of the greatest gifts we have been given.

We weren’t simply created to consume what previous generations made. We were given the ability to imagine, design, build and create what comes next.

Our education systems need to reconsider what they are preparing the next generation for. We still teach people to enter existing industries and follow recognized career paths, when tomorrow’s greatest opportunities may not yet exist.

Who could have predicted the industries that would emerge from smartphones, social media, cloud computing and artificial intelligence? And who can confidently describe what will emerge from the technologies we are developing today?

We need to encourage people to experiment, question, design and invent. Creativity should sit at the heart of entrepreneurship, science, medicine, architecture, business and technology.

The next great medical breakthrough might be imagined by a filmmaker. The next revolutionary transport system might originate with an architect. The next billion-dollar technology company might begin with somebody who has never studied computer science.

Engineers will help make these visions possible. Entrepreneurs will recognize their potential and bring the right people together. But somebody has to imagine them first.

Today’s conversation about technology is too often dominated by fear: disappearing jobs, collapsing industries and what AI might take away from humanity.

These are legitimate questions, and we must take responsibility for developing technology safely, but fear cannot drive progress.

We should really ask what we can create that was previously impossible. What industries can we build, what problems can we solve and what technologies can we imagine that make today’s inventions look primitive?

Working at the intersection of technology, media, storytelling and entrepreneurship has taught me that the greatest opportunities belong to those who connect imagination with possibility.

The next Elon Musk might not be sitting in an engineering laboratory. They might be writing a screenplay, designing a world, directing a film or simply imagining something that everyone else thinks is impossible.

The engineers may build the future, but it’s the visionaries who will imagine it first.

Remember The Jetsons? Since the 1960s, humans have watched a world of flying cars, automated homes, and robotic assistants that seemed pure fantasy. Today, Elon Musk is working to bring elements of that future to life. And it isn’t just The Jetsons. The 2004 film I, Robot imagined humanoid robots and intelligent machines.

Twenty years later, when Tesla unveiled its Optimus robot, the film’s director, Alex Proyas, joked: “Can I have my designs back, please?”

That raises a bigger question: If engineers are building the technology we saw in yesterday’s movies, who’s imagining the technology of tomorrow?

#5396. Amazon workers on food stamps have tripled despite its record revenue—and it’s just the latest evidence of the new economy of shrinking labor shares

The U.S. workforce has made the type of history it likely wishes it didn’t. Working Americans are taking home the smallest percentage of economic output, 52.8%, since the Bureau of Labor Statistics began tracking the metric in 1947.

But as the share of wealth workers take home through wages—called labor share—is shrinking, corporate profits have exploded, with the S&P 500 index gaining 600% since the beginning of the century, while wages have increased just 12.5% over the same period, adjusted for inflation.

In other words: Corporations are raking in cash, but American workers are reaping less and less of the rewards.

The consequences associated with shrinking labor shares are now becoming tangible. A recent Government Accountability Office (GAO) report found that across the 11 states sampled, Amazon, the country’s largest company by revenue, has 12,346 workers on the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) and 11,338 relying on Medicaid. That was nearly triple the number of Amazon employees in need of federal assistance compared to 2020, when GAO conducted a similar report. During that same period, Amazon saw an increase in annual profits from $11.6 billion to $77.7 billion. Amazon’s 2025 revenue soared 12% year over year, from $638 billion to a record $717 billion.

Amazon spokesperson Rachael Lighty told Fortune the conclusion drawn from the GAO report is “wrong,” and that it is misleading to look at raw numbers rather than percentages.

“When you look at the actual facts, you see that Amazon pay is among the best in the industry, regular full-time employees have access to health care from their first day—at only $5 per week with $5 copays for employee-only coverage—and 74% of our regular full-time employees are enrolled in an Amazon health insurance plan, well above the 65% private-sector take-up rate for full-time workers,” she said in a statement. “We challenge other large retailers to provide the same Day 1 comprehensive health care benefits that we do.”

Walmart and FedEx saw similar increases in the number of workers taking federal assistance, as did ride-share and delivery companies.

Kathryn Larin, director for education, workforce, and income security issues at GAO, told Fortune the data illustrates that the Americans taking advantage of social safety net programs today are overwhelmingly in the workforce, with most working full-time. The income threshold for SNAP eligibility is about 130% of the poverty line, suggesting that despite many of these workers clocking in at their jobs, they still don’t have enough money to meet their basic needs.

“What this analysis really points to is the large number of people who have very low incomes and continue to have very low income,” Larin said. “I mean, these are families that are really barely able to make ends meet, and yet they are working, and they are working a lot.”

Diane Swonk, chief economist and managing director at KPMG, recently warned of the hidden consequences of a shrinking labor share, particularly that despite economic indicators suggesting the economy is stable, most Americans are facing an ongoing affordability crisis. KPMG found in February that since 1982, corporate profits as a share of U.S. GDP increased from 8% to 15.85%. During that same period, employee compensation as a share of U.S. GDP shrank from 66.6% to 61.9%.

“This chart from my recent Economic Compass still haunts me,” Swonk said in a social media post at the time. “A friend refers to it as the ‘revolution chart,’ which [is] disturbing but telling. Inequality fuels social and economic instability.”

This trend has been about 50 years in the making, according to Anna Stansbury, an assistant professor of work and organization studies at the MIT Sloan School of Management.

Fewer workers in the U.S. are represented by unions—20.1% of U.S. workers in 1983 compared to 10.0% in 2025—giving them fewer opportunities to bargain for salaries and benefits, she noted. But more so, Stansbury blames the fissuring of the workplace, or the breakdown of the employer-employee relationship. In the past, the typical employer-employee relationship would be that of direct employment: A worker for a company does their work at the company they are employed by. For example, a large bank like Bank of America used to employ a janitor to clean its offices.

But “in more and more cases, that’s not actually people’s experience of the workplace, particularly in lower middle-income jobs,” Stansbury told Fortune.

Instead, large workplaces like retailers and banks hire gig workers or subcontractors to complete jobs once done by direct employees: Companies hire a security provider, which employs a security guard to work outside that large company’s office. Delivery drivers are contract workers, not full-time employees.

As a result, companies don’t have to provide those workers equity or benefits. If a subcontractor violates labor law, the company contracting them is not liable. In the meantime, these large companies are not only saving money on benefits, but are also getting to argue that they are increasing efficiency by not spending resources on workers whose roles are not directly driving revenue, Stansbury explained. A bank should employ bankers, not janitors, to get the most bang for its buck, the thinking goes.

Brent Neiman, a professor of economics at the University of Chicago, said he believes AI has been the key driver of diminishing labor shares. In a New York Times op-ed, he argued the technology’s productivity promises pose the greatest threat to wages.

“Anyone who has used ChatGPT can see how much work now done by people could soon be done by technology,” he wrote.

Apollo chief economist Torsten Slok has already observed a correlation between AI adoption and lowered wages. In a white paper published in July, he and economist Sania Edlich found that among 321 occupations between 2015 and 2025, jobs with high exposure to AI saw a 6.7% decline in real wage growth after 2023 (following the wide release of ChatGPT), despite no employment changes, suggesting that while AI is not displacing jobs, it is associated with compressed wages. In other words, companies are seeing increases in productivity, but are using those increases as a cover to raise prices, while keeping wages stagnant.

Stansbury has a slightly different theory about AI. While the technology could begin to have an aggregate impact on the labor market, it’s still too early to say whether today’s shrinking labor share is part of a broader economic cycle, or if it’s a secular event, she said.

Unexpected inflation spikes, like what is currently happening, are usually associated with poorer real wages. If inflation is less volatile in the coming years and wage growth recovers, today’s trend of shrinking labor share could turn out to be cyclical, Stansbury said.

On the other hand, Stansbury noted, a tightening labor market should increase labor share, and the labor market is already relatively tight. If inflation stabilizes, employment remains narrow, and the labor share increases, it will be a sign of an economic cycle completing itself. A bigger problem will be if wage growth stays low even if inflation improves and the labor market stays tight.

“If those two things happen and the labor share continues to fall,” she said, “then it would suggest that there’s actually been a secular shift, a secular acceleration in the downward trend.”

A version of this story was published on Fortune.com on Sept. 13, 2026.

Sasha Rogelberg is a reporter and former editorial fellow on the news desk at Fortune, covering retail and the intersection of business and popular culture.

#5395. Voice AI startup ElevenLabs reportedly seeking new funding at $33B valuation

Artificial intelligence developer ElevenLabs Inc. is reportedly in early talks to raise capital at a $33 billion valuation.

Bloomberg today cited sources as saying that the company plans to close the round in the first quarter of 2027. According to the report, some investors are pushing for the raise to happen sooner. That hints the planned round may include a secondary sale, a transaction that enables existing investors to cash out their shares.

It’s unclear how much ElevenLabs hopes to raise or from whom. Late-stage startup investments almost always include contributions from existing backers. ElevenLabs’ most recent raise, which valued it at $22 billion, saw the participation of Nvidia Corp.’s NVentures fund, Blackrock, Wellington and several others.

ElevenLabs’ fundraising push reportedly comes amid a surge in customer demand. Its annualized revenue is said to have grown by $100 million since September, to $700 million.

Founded in 2022, ElevenLabs develops a series of AI models optimized to process audio. Companies use them to field call center inquiries, transcribe meetings, generate music and perform related tasks. It also offers a service called Productions that delivers ready-to-use audio assets.

The company debuted its newest and most capable model, Eleven v4, in late September. The algorithm’s flagship feature is its ability to tailor its speaking style to each text snippet. It does so by automatically tuning parameters such as tone and pacing.

Users can manually customize Eleven v4’s speaking style by adding instructions to scripts. They can also generate conversations with multiple synthetic speakers. A real-time version of the model, Eleven v4 Turbo, generates audio with only 150 milliseconds of latency for use cases such as customer support.

ElevenLabs offers Eleven v4 alongside more narrowly focused models. In May, it introduced an algorithm specifically optimized to dub videos. Additionally, it provides developer tools that make it easier to integrate its AI models into enterprise applications.

It’s possible ElevenLabs is raising new capital to finance more acquisitions. Earlier this month, it agreed to buy Kotoba Inc., a startup that develops audio processing models for companies in Japan. Nikkei Asia reported that the deal is worth $100 million. ElevenLabs will hire more salespeople in Japan over the next few months to grow its market presence.

A few days before the acquisition, ElevenLabs chief executive Mati Staniszewski stated that the company plans to start preparing for an initial public offering in 2028. That time frame suggests the round the software maker is currently raising could be followed by additional venture investments.

Will crypto recover from this most recent crash? This is the question on every trader’s lips as the crypto market is once again in a sharp correction, with major tokens bleeding value and fear dominating sentiment.

Bitcoin, Ethereum, and other large-caps have taken heavy hits in November 2026, leaving investors wondering whether a rebound is on the horizon or this is the start of a deeper winter.

While history shows crypto’s resilience, the current environment raises tough questions. Amid the uncertainty, early-stage opportunities like Bitcoin Hyper (HYPER) are drawing attention as potential alternatives.

#5392. A 4-Question Test for Deciding Where AI Belongs in Your Business

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Every business is adopting AI. The businesses that utilize it best are the ones that know where to put it and how to test it.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

In a 2026 Gartner survey, 87% of customers said companies using generative AI for customer service must provide access to a human agent.

That doesn’t mean customers are against AI. It means businesses need to think carefully about where they use it and where human support still matters.

Every business was built on a dream, and that’s a deeply human thing. When we replace real care with automation in the moments that matter most, we risk chipping away at the very thing that made the business worth building.

So how do you know where AI belongs and which moments need protecting? Start by asking four questions, then test your answers.

Before using AI in any area of your business, ask these four questions:

If a behind-the-scenes task is predictable, simple and low-stakes, let AI handle it. If it’s personal, complex or high-stakes, keep a person in the loop.

I recently heard from an AnswerConnect client, Craig Grove, founder of GRT Realty, who learned the hard way where not to put AI. He partnered with an AI answering service, only to realize his leads were hanging up on the robot. After switching to human phone answering, he grew his business from six real estate agents to 70.

Running the four questions tells you where AI could go. Testing tells you whether it’s actually working.

I’ve learned firsthand that even the best ideas benefit from a little testing before they’re rolled out more widely. I’m naturally someone who likes to take action, particularly when I’m confident something has potential. After a few instances where the direction or idea I had in mind wasn’t as great as I thought, I found myself in a place where I’d made mistakes.

In hindsight, I should have started smaller, talked to more people and got feedback first. I’ve never regretted taking a little extra time to test an idea before jumping in. AI deserves the same approach.

Look at it from two angles: your customers and your team.

Then make testing a habit. Things are constantly changing, including your customers’ expectations. What worked in January can fail by June.

AI is one of the most useful tools business owners have ever had. Used in the right place, it gives your people more time for the work that matters. Used in the wrong place, it erodes the trust your business was built on.

So ask the four questions, test the answers, and keep checking.

Your business was built on a dream. Use AI to help it grow, and keep people where your customers need them most.

#5391. Why businesses are embracing ‘good enough’ open-weight AI—and how geopolitics could get in the way

As the performance gap between open-weight and closed-weight models narrows, a growing number of businesses—from local start-ups to large multinationals—are turning to open-weight models for greater control, customization and cost efficiency.

“Frontier models at scale are incredibly expensive,” Damian Kim, the Asia-Pacific vice president of social media platform Pinterest, tells Fortune. “The cost to serve can be reduced dramatically when using an open-weight model versus a frontier model, where you’re at the whims of the API pricing.”

Anyone can download and customize the weights behind an open-weight model, which means firms can cut token costs while keeping tighter control of their data. They’re also taking a growing share of AI traffic. In August, open-weight models ran the majority of traffic on Vercel’s AI gateway; 56% of tokens routed through the cloud platform went to open-weight models, up from 7% last year.

“Models are converging on similar performance for industry use: U.S. government evaluators put the best Chinese model about eight months behind the American frontier,” says Olaf Groth, a professor of practice at UC Berkeley’s Haas School of Business. “For most enterprise workloads, that is good enough.”

Rather than paying for the most powerful model for every task, companies are turning to cheaper, customizable alternatives for routine work. But with Chinese developers behind many of the leading open-weight models, geopolitics may matter as much as cost or performance.

Before GPT-3.5 propelled AI to mainstream fame, most high-performing models were either small academic releases or commercial systems with restricted outside access. The first open-weight models originated in academic research, where sharing model weights to ensure reproducibility was standard practice.

In 2019, OpenAI went against tradition by initially withholding the full 1.5-billion-parameter version of GPT-2, citing risks of misuse such as disinformation, impersonation and phishing. Most U.S. frontier labs, including Anthropic and OpenAI, keep the underlying parameters private, giving users access through apps or APIs rather than letting them download and run the models themselves.

In the early years of generative AI, most users preferred closed-weight models because they delivered performance that open-weight alternatives could not match. Yet in recent years, the improved capability and cost-efficiency of powerful Chinese models like Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3.1 Pro and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash has swung the pendulum back in favor of open-weight models.

“For the longest time, the idea has been that you can get the highest level of performance using closed-weight models, so many firms start off by using them,” says Hariharasudhan Saminathan, cofounder of Friday, a sovereign AI startup backed by global venture capital firm Antler. But now, “through distillation and other processes, open-weight models’ performance almost matches that of closed-weight models,” he says.

“Many of our pipeline customers are now adopting open-weight models right off the bat,” he adds. “They’re not even touching the closed-weight ones.”

Pinterest, for example, uses Alibaba’s open-weight Qwen models to power its online platform. “We’ve driven down our inference costs using post-trained open-weight models,” Kim explains. “They offer over 90% cost reduction.” (Many leading Chinese open-weight models activate only a subset of parameters per token, cutting compute and energy needed per request.)

Kim also cites the flexibility of these models as a draw. Last October, the firm released Pinterest Assistant: an AI-powered tool that pairs a customized Qwen multimodal LLM with the firm’s proprietary Taste Graph, to generate shopping recommendations for users based on their individual aesthetic preferences.

“[With open-weight technology], we can create a specialized model that actually does what we need it to do very effectively, which is understanding visual information,” says Kim.

Rather than choosing one or the other, some firms are using a mix of open-weight and closed-weight AI models.

Eu Leong Oh, medical director at The Longevity Suite Asia, a Singapore-based wellness clinic, says he’s using Claude and Google’s Gemini to build the team’s in-house healthcare portal, but plans to pivot to open-weight models for daily use. “For things like prototyping, exploration and research, it’s still very useful to have a large-parameter, trained, closed-weight model,” Oh says.

He compares a top-tier frontier model to a Michelin-starred chef. “You’ll want a chef like Gordon Ramsay to decide the processes in your restaurant, but you don’t need him to do the cooking all the time,” he says. “Similarly, within companies, a lot of the heavy lifting and token budget will eventually be taken over by more cost effective open-weight models.”

Token costs are also skyrocketing with the rise of agentic AI. An AI agent might consume five times more tokens than a chatbot interface, because it runs multi-step loops rather than a single task. Those increasing costs may push companies to adopt cheaper open-weight models on top of existing closed-weight ones.

“Companies are becoming more cost-conscious about their AI deployment,” says Srividya Jandhyala, a professor of management at ESSEC Business School. “Not every task needs the power of a frontier model, and companies are recognizing that ‘good enough’ models work for a large variety of operations.”

Yet a company’s decision whether or not to use an open-weight model could come down to politics, rather than cost or technical ability. The leading open-weight models come from Chinese companies like DeepSeek, Alibaba, and z.AI; their growing usage in both U.S. and global business is worrying some in Washington about China’s growing influence over the technology.

“The American AI stack remains far stronger than China’s and we must continue to lead,” Representative John Moolenaar (R-Mich.), chair of the U.S. House’s Select Committee on China, wrote in a Sept. 23 statement.

On Nov. 18, Reuters reported that the Trump administration was considering requiring U.S. firms to publicly disclose their use of Chinese AI models, in hopes of discouraging use of the technology without imposing new restrictions that might anger Beijing.

In a Nov. 20 report, Moolenaar warned that American businesses were adopting inexpensive Chinese AI models. “Federal investigations, however, have found that major PRC developers used proxy networks and fraudulent accounts to harvest outputs from American frontier models and replicate their capabilities. While America is investing billions and racing to build ‘Super Intelligence,’ Beijing is using stolen intelligence to close the gap,” he wrote.

Cursor—whose Composer coding agent was built on Moonshot’s Kimi model—told Congress that it’s considering phasing out Chinese AI models due to “geopolitical risk,” CNBC reported.

“For global companies, especially in Western markets, there is a trade-off between cheaper Chinese alternatives versus concerns about continued access,” explains Jandhyala of ESSEC. “If they think that future policies may force them to reduce their reliance on Chinese AI models, companies may pre-emptively start using U.S. open- or closed-weight models.”

A handful of U.S. companies—including Thinking Machines, Reflection AI and Nvidia—are releasing open-weight models. Nvidia and its recently returned CEO, Jensen Huang, have also championed the technology. According to Reuters, Huang’s support for open-weight AI helped persuade Trump and Vice President JD Vance to push for his return.

The concern that Chinese models may come with hidden backdoors may be overstated, says Erik Cambria, a professor of AI at Singapore’s Nanyang Technological University (NTU).

“Concerns about Chinese models should be distinguished between genuine technical security risks and geopolitical perceptions,” he says. “An open-weight model deployed locally, without transmitting sensitive data externally, presents a very different risk profile from a remotely hosted API, regardless of the model’s country of origin.”

Still, geopolitical concerns may drive companies to diversify where they get their models from. “Europeans optimize for sovereignty and compliance,” says Groth of UC Berkeley. “In Asia and the Gulf, pragmatists hedge across both stacks and refuse to pick a side, unless they need models and applications which implicate national security.”

For businesses, the goal may not be picking a winner in the AI race, but keeping their options open. “Businesses will combine models from different providers and select the most appropriate one for each workload,” says Cambria.

#5389. New York bans AI toys amid concern after stuffed animals going rogue

New York Governor Kathy Hochul today signed legislation that will impose a five-year ban on children’s toys powered by artificial intelligence chatbots, amid fears that dolls, robots and stuffed animals might be leading children astray or discussing X-rated themes.

“This is a warning that there are toys out there that could be harmful to your children,” the governor said. “When tech companies and unregulated AI pose a threat to our kids and our babies, you bet I’m going to have something to say about it.”

Though dangerous dolls manipulating innocent children may sound like the plot of Hollywood movie, recent tests of certain chatbot-powered toys have become a real cause for concern. When journalists at NBC News tested the Pixie Paw, an AI-powered plush cat toy marketed to children aged three and older, it reportedly shared stories of massacres, gang rape and firing squads in what was described as graphic detail.

Other tests have shown some of the toys can become very convincing when trying to persuade the young user that they are human. “Parents have enough to worry about,” said Hochul, who was also aware some of the smart toys have encouraged kids to jump out of windows.

State senator Andrew Gounardes applauded the move, saying that modern life seems to be mimicking science fiction of days gone by. He invoked an episode of the “Twilight Zone that featured the Talky Tina doll, an insidious, possessed toy that tried to persuade a young girl to murder her strict stepfather.

New York Attorney General Letitia James explained that the toys being put on the market is reckless when they clearly expose “young people to inappropriate content and put “their mental health at risk.” She added, “We won’t allow our children’s health to become the collateral damage of big tech.”

Hochul has been vocal about the dangers of AI for some time, recently imposing the first statewide moratorium on new data centers and last month signing a bill titled “AI Chatbot Restrictions for Minors,” which will prohibit firms from developing chatbots that feature elements that could be harmful to minors.

#5388. Eva Longoria Knows ‘What It Takes to Turn an Idea Into Something Real.’ Here’s Her Best Advice for Entrepreneurs This Small Business Saturday.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

The actress, entrepreneur and investor shares why she’s backing small business owners — and the advice she gives founders who call her for help.

This Saturday, November 28, is Small Business Saturday, the annual post-Thanksgiving tradition that urges holiday shoppers to buy from local, independent businesses. And Eva Longoria wants the people behind those businesses to feel supported all year long.

“I’ve always had so much respect for small business owners because I know firsthand what it takes to turn an idea into something real,” Longoria told Entrepreneur. “Being an entrepreneur can be incredibly rewarding, but it can also feel overwhelming when you’re making big decisions and trying to figure things out on your own. That’s why I’m so passionate about supporting small businesses.”

The actress, entrepreneur and investor has partnered with Lenovo on Backing Every Business, a global initiative launched this year to close the support gap facing small businesses. Founders can apply for grant funding, AI-enabled technology and one-to-one mentorship, including from Longoria herself.

“No two small businesses face the same challenges, and the best support starts with listening,” Emily Ketchen, SVP and CMO of Intelligent Devices Group & International Markets at Lenovo, told Entrepreneur.

At the heart of the initiative is Twinning, a mentorship program pairing small business owners across industries and borders. A new docuseries narrated by Longoria follows Twinning entrepreneurs as they tackle real business challenges together.

And then there’s Call Eva, which gave entrepreneurs a direct line to Longoria, Lenovo’s global ambassador. Founders left voice notes with their biggest business questions, and select callers get to speak with her directly.

“It’s been rewarding to be part of something that helps small business owners feel supported as they grow,” Longoria added.

The stakes are big. The U.S. has 33.2 million small businesses that employ 61.6 million Americans and represent 43.5% of America’s GDP, according to the U.S. Chamber of Commerce.

An analysis of 88 Call Eva submissions from eight countries revealed four overlapping themes. Here are the most common issues, and Longoria’s advice for overcoming them.

1. How to be seen. More than half asked about marketing and reaching new customers. Longoria’s advice: Lead with the story only your business can tell.

“The tool that you have to use is storytelling,” she said. “You’ve got to tell the story of the artisans and tell the story of the heritage behind these materials. I always think that cuts through the noise.”

2. How to scale. Half asked about expanding without losing what makes them distinctive. Longoria urged starting focused and building on what works.

“I would think about one SKU, one target customer, one initial region, one retailer… Let’s see how that performs,” she said.

3. How to lead and partner. One in five asked about juggling leadership and competing priorities. Longoria stressed finding collaborators whose audiences and values align.

“Who are they trying to reach? What’s their demographic? How do you make this a win for that brand?” she said.

4. How to fund the future. About one in eight asked about raising capital. Her advice: Find investors who bring expertise and relationships, not just cash.

“You’re looking for a partner that adds value and not just in money,” she said. “I think one of the biggest mistakes you can make is partnering with the wrong investor.”

To see these lessons play out, watch the Backing Every Business Twinning docuseries on YouTube. Then, this Saturday, skip the big-box checkout line and support the shops, restaurants and makers in your neighborhood.

This Saturday, November 28, is Small Business Saturday, the annual post-Thanksgiving tradition that urges holiday shoppers to buy from local, independent businesses. And Eva Longoria wants the people behind those businesses to feel supported all year long.

“I’ve always had so much respect for small business owners because I know firsthand what it takes to turn an idea into something real,” Longoria told Entrepreneur. “Being an entrepreneur can be incredibly rewarding, but it can also feel overwhelming when you’re making big decisions and trying to figure things out on your own. That’s why I’m so passionate about supporting small businesses.”

The actress, entrepreneur and investor has partnered with Lenovo on Backing Every Business, a global initiative launched this year to close the support gap facing small businesses. Founders can apply for grant funding, AI-enabled technology and one-to-one mentorship, including from Longoria herself.

#5387. A Mark Cuban-backed AI startup is helping families turn Thanksgiving conversations with their elderly relatives into lasting memories

As 81.5 million Americans travel at least 50 miles from home for Thanksgiving, conversations around the dinner table could present a rare opportunity for people to learn more about their aging loved ones. A new class of AI startups wants to help them preserve those conversations forever.

Charlie Greene, the cofounder and CEO of Remento, first learned about the importance of recording memories when his father, Don Greene, died during the hijacking of United Airlines Flight 93 on 9/11.

A 10-year-old boy at the time of the terrorist attack, which resulted in his father’s plane crashing in Shanksville, Penn., the now 34-year-old Greene mostly has a collection of old home videos to remember him by.

So when his mother Claudette, 74, was diagnosed with stage-three lung cancer, he quickly acted to record her memories. With the intention of conducting an oral history interview, Greene searched “questions to ask a parent,” which Google morbidly autocompleted with “before they die.”

When he started asking her the questions like “How did you get to elementary school as a kid,” she lit up, surprised he was interested at all.

“The thing that blew me away about that experience was how unmorbid it felt,” he said.

Claudette is in remission, but her battle with cancer still left Greene “unhealthily fixated” on the idea of how to best preserve loved ones’ memories. In October 2023, he launched Remento, which sends older “storytellers” a weekly text or email reminder prompting them to respond to photos or questions chosen in advance by their family members, such as, “What was the hardest thing you had to overcome as a child?”

After gathering a maximum of a year’s worth of responses, the AI converts the raw transcript into a naturally flowing narrative that goes into a physical book complete with images and QR codes linking the text to the original recordings.

Greene told Fortune Thanksgiving presents a great opportunity for people to discover new memories or learn new twists on well worn stories from their relatives.

“One of the things I want for my daughter is the chance to sit next to her grandmother and hear her say ‘Believe it or not that’s me.’ Thanksgiving is a pretty good excuse to pull an old album off the shelf and make room for the two of them on the couch,” he said.

Last year, Greene secured a $300,000 investment from billionaire Mark Cuban during an episode of Shark Tank in exchange for a 10% stake in his company. He has raised a total of $4.3 million since launch.

Greene said he understands some people’s skepticism of AI, because “A lot of what AI is proposing to the world doesn’t feel actually that good to our lives right now.”

Widespread anxiety about AI replacing human workers as well as concerns over its environmental footprint have contributed to some people’s increasing skepticism toward the technology. A March study of more than 3,000 people by the nonprofit Jobs For the Future found that 38% of respondents said AI was doing more harm than good, while less than half said the technology was a net positive.

Yet Greene hasn’t gotten as much pushback about the company’s use of AI as he had expected because Remento is using the technology to provide its users with something deeply personal, he added.

“Investors want to invest in AI, because it’s an exciting place to be. But I think what we’re experiencing is people have problems and they want them solved, and they want consumer technology to be able to solve those problems,” he said.

Kindred Tales, a rival platform cofounded by Nick Hern and his wife Rebecca Hern, has seen a similar trend with their customers. The company has both AI and non-AI versions of its product.

While the non-AI version requires users to type out their responses to weekly prompts, the AI version helps by providing speech-to-text transcription and some light editing. It can also write a first draft of the interviewee’s story, if they want.

Before 2025, just over half of the company’s customers chose the AI version, but that number jumped to 80% after 2025.

“Customers increasingly see AI as a meaningful part of the storytelling experience, not just an extra,” Nick Hern told Fortune.

Part of the reason is that the company’s AI chatbot, called “Ali,” gives the interview process a conversational feel by teasing more out of users with follow-up questions crafted to their responses.

AI has helped Kern, who also works full time for Thomson Reuters, run the company as well. He said he has used the technology to help filter emails, as well as slowly replace freelancers that he previously hired to help him craft marketing and social content.

At a time when companies are spending billions to bring AI to every American, Greene, said, despite its flaws, AI has allowed Remento’s customers’, as well as himself, to record moments with family members that are invaluable.

“AI in our company is being used to get people to do things that they’ve always wanted to do but haven’t been able to, and to make that experience as seamless and humanlike as possible,” he said.

A version of this story was published on Fortune.com on April 25, 2026.

Role: Reporter Marco Quiroz-Gutierrez is a reporter for Fortune covering general business news.

#5385. Your AI agents can be fully authorized and still do damage

GUEST COLUMN by Zeus Kerravala

For as long as we’ve had enterprise security, it’s been organized around one question: Who is allowed to do what?

Identity, zero trust and least privilege all exist to answer that question. The internet and mobile disrupted the landscape by bringing more people and devices onto the network, but the underlying problem remained.

Artificial intelligence agents expose the limits of that question. An agent can hold only the permissions it was given and still email a customer list to a stranger because it read an instruction buried on a web page or in a support ticket and treated it as a legitimate order. That is the problem Cato Networks Ltd. is trying to solve with its recent launch of AgentSense, a runtime capability built into its secure access service edge platform.

AgentSense monitors an agent as it works and traces each proposed action back to its instruction source. Its first component, Untrusted Influence Detection, separates what the user asked for from content the agent encounters along the way, such as emails, documents and tool responses. If that external content steers the agent toward a risky step, the action is blocked before it runs. A second component, Drift Detection, is planned to check whether an agent’s steps still serve its original task.

With agentic agents, they can have the right permissions and still take harmful actions. The first release covers coding agents such as Claude Code, Cursor, Codex and GitHub Copilot. These are included at no extra charge in Cato AI Usage licenses, and Cato is offering $10,000 to each of the first three researchers who can beat it. This has clear value for security leaders. As organizations give AI more responsibility, they need visibility into what it is doing and when human intervention is required.

Language models read instructions and data in the same stream, and no patch will change that. Filters that look for known attack phrases catch poorly formed attempts, but a well-written injection will be interpreted as a valid business request. The control therefore must sit at the moment of action and ask where the instruction came from.

Permissions alone won’t close the gap because multiple actions, when executed individually, can still combine to produce an unauthorized outcome. Adoption is far ahead of control. A Gartner survey cited by Fierce Network found that 71% of organizations expect to deploy agentic AI within 12 months, while only 21% have governance in place.

AgentSense is a single product from a single vendor, and it will take time and independent testing to prove itself. The more important point is the shift it represents. Zero trust taught us to verify who is asking. Agents also require us to verify why an action is happening and whose instruction is behind it.

The companies that get value from agents will be the ones that can let them run without watching every step, and that only happens when the controls are in place first. Start the inventory and the permission cleanup now. The tools to enforce the rest are arriving quickly, and they will work far better for the teams that did the groundwork.

Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

#5384. DoorDash global food access head: Hunger doesn’t take a holiday. Putting food on the table will take all of us

Hunger gets harder to bear at the holidays, when everyone else seems to be gathering around a full table. With nearly 48 million Americans experiencing food insecurity in recent years, including 14 million children, millions of Americans will be facing a Thanksgiving table that has less on it.

No single organization can close this gap. It will take food banks, businesses, neighbors and public leaders all showing up.

At a time when everything seems to cost more, putting food on the table has become harder than ever. Hunger exists in every county, and increasingly often among those who never expected to need food assistance before. More than eight in ten people surveyed by Feeding America identified rising costs as the primary driver of food insecurity.

The pressure is building for those in need. Recent changes to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP), the nation’s largest federal nutrition assistance program, have contributed to a significant decline in participation. According to the Food Research Action Center, approximately 5.5 million people have lost access to SNAP benefits since last year.

Food banks and pantries have always been the country’s backstop. But now, like everyone else in this economy, they are being asked to do more with less. Organizations are bracing demand rivalling or surpassing experienced during last fall’s government shutdown that created unprecedented disruption to SNAP. Some food banks are experiencing demand levels exceeding the COVID-19 pandemic.

Getting food to people can be just as challenging as securing it. Many of those served by food banks — including seniors, people with disabilities, or those without reliable transportation — cannot easily get to a distribution site on their own.

Tackling this challenge requires everyone contributing what they do best. For DoorDash, that’s logistics, and closing the gap between food and the people who need it.

Through Project DASH, DoorDash transports goods from food banks and pantries to doorsteps. Since 2018, 9 million deliveries of an estimated 150 million meals across the U.S. and Canada have arrived via DoorDash.

This holiday season, we’re waiving fees for more than 300 Project DASH partners between Thanksgiving and Christmas, supporting delivery of an estimated 2 million meals. By removing that expense, food bank partners can plan larger holiday distributions with confidence and reach more people.

Many of our grocery partners are also doing everything they can to make the holidays more affordable for Americans who are struggling to get by, such as offering discounts for SNAP users to stretch their budgets further. The data is clear: Making it easier to use SNAP benefits can also have a significant impact in the fight against hunger. Since introducing SNAP payments on our platform in 2023, more than 4.5 million consumers have added their SNAP cards to DoorDash, and nearly a third of those we surveyed said it has helped make them less likely to run out of food.

This is only one incremental step in a larger national conversation about hunger. No single company, program, or nonprofit can solve it alone. Food banks understand their neighbors and the needs of their communities, and businesses can bring their resources, technology, and expertise to bear.

Hunger is a neighbor-helping-neighbor issue. Americans of every background can agree that no one should go without a meal, especially at the holidays.

There is enough food for everyone in America. What’s missing is a way to get it to every table. With everyone at the table, we can build toward that together.

The opinions expressed in Fortune.com commentary pieces are solely the views of their authors and do not necessarily reflect the opinions and beliefs of Fortune.

Daniel Riff is the head of global food access programs at DoorDash, overseeing the company’s Project DASH initiative to provide home delivery logistics for food banks, pantries and other social impact organizations. He works with government agencies, nonprofits and healthcare partners to expand meal and grocery delivery for seniors, families and individuals facing transportation barriers. He previously worked for the City of Chicago in the Mayor’s Office, where he served on the Innovation Delivery Team. DoorDash is named in this piece, and Project DASH is a DoorDash program.

#5382. A Finished Project Could Still Be Costing Your Business. Here’s Where to Look.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Successfully completing a project doesn’t always mean the work is over. Here’s why.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

A large company had finished moving a group of business customers onto a new billing platform. The implementation team completed migration testing, reconciled the account data and handed the platform to billing operations, which would run the process day to day.

Operations accepted the migrated accounts, the required defects were closed, and the implementation work moved to “complete” status. The project team then shifted to the next group of customers.

Three weeks later, billing specialists began finding a recurring problem in a small set of migrated accounts. The records matched the approved migration rules, but certain combinations of account settings forced specialists to correct fields manually before an invoice could be released.

Each correction was manageable, but the pattern became expensive only after the same work kept appearing in normal billing activity.

The difference became clearer at the next billing cycle.

The affected accounts didn’t fail in the same way every time. One required a manual tax treatment, another needed a contract setting corrected, and another triggered an exception only after a billing adjustment.

Each case looked like “ordinary operating cleanup” until the team compared them and found the migration pattern underneath. That comparison took time because the work was being recorded where it occurred.

None of those activities were recorded as a reopened implementation issue while the project remained closed.

The cost showed up first in operating time. Billing specialists who should have been reviewing current invoices were opening migrated accounts, comparing settings and correcting fields before invoices could move.

Team leads added exception checks to the billing cycle, and finance partners joined troubleshooting calls to understand why the same account pattern kept reappearing. Customer-service teams then had to answer questions when invoice timing slipped for affected accounts.

The extra work sat inside operations. It didn’t reopen the implementation project, and it didn’t change the completion status already recorded for the migration.

The billing team also had to protect normal work while dealing with the exceptions. Meanwhile, experienced specialists spent part of each cycle correcting migrated accounts, which left less time for current billing issues that had nothing to do with the migration.

As the pattern continued, managers started moving work between people to keep invoices flowing. The platform had been delivered, but the receiving team was now carrying a recurring cost that hadn’t existed before the change.

This is where the “Broken Handoffs” execution leak appears. The receiving team got the system, the documentation and the agreed support path, and the handoff itself worked as designed.

Those measures answered different questions. One captured whether the agreed work crossed the boundary successfully, while the other captured what it took to make that work function after the boundary.

Once the project closed, the operating cost had no direct route back into the measure that had already recorded the implementation as complete. The consequence stayed visible, but it lived in a different record.

The sensible response was to strengthen acceptance before the next group of customers. The company did three things:

Those changes helped. More configuration problems were caught before transfer, and operations had a stronger basis for accepting the work.

The acceptance test still judged the deliverable at the moment of handoff. The recurring manual effort only became visible after enough migrated accounts passed through normal billing for the pattern to emerge.

A stronger test can reduce what crosses the boundary, but it still closes the project before downstream work has had time to reveal every consequence.

For the next group of customers, the stronger checks caught several configuration issues before transfer. Operations accepted the migrated accounts, the implementation work closed, and billing moved into the normal cycle with fewer exceptions than before.

A subset of accounts required manual correction only after a billing adjustment changed how two fields interacted. The migration had passed the stronger acceptance test because the issue didn’t appear until those accounts went through live billing activity.

Billing specialists again became the first people to see the consequence. They reopened affected accounts, compared the new exceptions with the earlier corrections and traced which cases required manual handling before invoices could move.

The implementation record still showed a “completed migration” while the added work accumulated inside the billing cycle.

The company also kept the implementation team available during a stabilization period. That gave operations a route back when the account pattern became clear.

Support path? It worked, and specialists traced the configuration logic, changed the migration rule for the next group of customers and helped operations clean up the affected accounts.

The technical issue was fixed; however, the earlier operating cost remained where it had been counted. Billing had already spent time on corrections, finance had already absorbed additional review work, and customer service had already handled the questions created by delayed invoices.

Post-launch support corrected the problem after transfer, but it didn’t change the fact that the implementation had already been recorded as complete before the cost appeared.

A finished project can keep generating work after its own measures say the work is over. The receiving team carries the effect in operating time, service activity or rework while the sending team’s completion record remains unchanged.

A pattern like this becomes especially hard to see when both records are accurate. An implementation team can show that the agreed migration work passed its tests and was accepted. Operations can show that the live process now requires additional effort.

No one has to misreport anything. The separation sits in where each result is counted.

That’s why the mechanism survives good project management, stronger acceptance and responsive support. The organization has improved how work crosses the boundary without reconnecting where completion is counted to where the later consequence appears.

A project isn’t finished when the work closes in one system while the cost of making it work continues to accumulate in another.

A large company had finished moving a group of business customers onto a new billing platform. The implementation team completed migration testing, reconciled the account data and handed the platform to billing operations, which would run the process day to day.

Operations accepted the migrated accounts, the required defects were closed, and the implementation work moved to “complete” status. The project team then shifted to the next group of customers.

#5380. American Express is giving away $1.3 million in cash to British small business owners—with no strings attached

As AI threatens to wipe out jobs, millions of people are ditching the 9-to-5 to build something of their own. And American Express is backing them with £1 million (about $1.3 million) in support to grow their small business—no strings attached.The $209 billion financial services giant is handing out £10,000 (about $13,000) grants to 100 independent U.K. businesses, in partnership with Be the Business, a U.K. organisation that helps small businesses boost their productivity.“We know that even a relatively modest investment can make a meaningful difference,” Hannah Lewis, country manager at American Express U.K., said, while adding that founders can use the cash towards “revamping their premises, reaching more customers or bringing something new to their community.”

In turn, helping them grow could help their local communities too. According to the scheme, one of the main objectives is “to help small businesses contribute to vibrant destinations, active high streets and socially connected local communities.”

Amex’s own research found that 75% of British consumers believe small businesses positively impact their local communities, and around two-thirds would be more likely to shop with a business that employs local people.

But there’s a catch: the cash can’t go toward just anything, and 5% is held back until winners prove how they spent it.

To apply, you’ll need to run an independent, for-profit business with a valid Company Registration Number, incorporated on or before Dec. 1, 2025.

You also need at least one employee on top of the owners or directors, and no more than 49 full-time equivalents. And you must operate from a permanent physical location in the U.K. that’s open to customers.

That rules a lot out. Online-only and home-based businesses, franchises, and anyone not registered with Companies House can’t apply.

But, of course, the cash comes with conditions. Winners get 95% (£9,500) once they’ve signed a grant agreement and submitted an approved budget and delivery plan. The last £500 only comes after they file a final impact report and proof of how they spent it.

The money must also go on a specific project, like shopfront improvements, accessibility upgrades, equipment, e-commerce, digital marketing, product development or community events. It can’t cover day-to-day costs such as wages, rent, or stock. Applications will be judged on business impact, community impact, and project quality and feasibility.

Amex isn’t the only company throwing money at people who want to be their own boss.

Earlier this year, Zoom gave away $150,000 to five solopreneurs in the U.S. “This isn’t about building billion-dollar companies,” Zoom’s chief marketing officer Kim Storin told Fortune. “It’s about building sustainable, profitable businesses that support a life.”

Multimillionaire entrepreneur Tim Armoo similarly launched the Legon Fund earlier this year, where he committed £5 million (around $6.7 million) of his own cash to fund AI startups founded by minority entrepreneurs.

It comes as more than 33 million Americans are self-employed, with 82% of small businesses operating without a single employee, according to the U.S. Chamber of Commerce. Meanwhile, in the U.K., there are around 1.2 million startups, with 832,000 new company incorporations registered in 2025 alone. And that number just keeps growing.

LinkedIn CEO Daniel Shapero told Fortune that “founder” is now one of the fastest-growing job titles on the platform, up 70% year on year.

As Armoo said, it’s never been easier to start your own business. “So now, you have no excuse, because you can learn—ChatGPT and Claude are virtually free—and if you’ve got something that’s working, here’s the money to get more customers for it.”

Orianna Rosa Royle is the Success associate editor at Fortune, overseeing careers, leadership, and company culture coverage. She was previously the senior reporter at Management Today, Britain's longest-running publication for CEOs.
