#5378. Your Plan for Next Year Could Be in Trouble Before It Even Begins — Unless You Ask the Right Question

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Unfinished work from this year consumes next year’s people and budget without appearing among the new priorities leaders are asked to rank.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

A large business unit was entering its annual planning cycle with three new priorities competing for specialist capacity. The leadership team had already reduced the list once, and the remaining proposals had strong business cases, clear owners and estimated resource needs.

The planning baseline also showed an older regulatory-remediation program that would continue into the new year. Nobody had forgotten it. The work was visible, funded and already staffed because the program had missed its original completion date.

During the planning session, one executive asked whether the remediation program would release its specialists early enough for the new priorities to start as planned. The program lead said the current end date still held unless the final regulatory review produced additional work. The room accepted that date and returned to ranking the new priorities, treating the remediation capacity as already committed until then.

What the planning discussion didn’t do was force the remediation work to compete again with the three new priorities. It sat in the baseline as committed work, while leaders debated how to allocate what they believed was the remaining capacity.

By the end of the session, the team had made disciplined choices:

The problem became visible in the first weeks of execution. One of the approved priorities needed several of the same risk, legal and data specialists who were still closing the remediation program.

The planning model counted those people as partially available because the older work was expected to wind down early in the year. Instead, a final set of regulatory findings required more analysis, and a small group of specialists stayed fully engaged.

The new priority still had its approved funding, executive sponsor and start date. The people needed to move it weren’t actually free.

The old work was visible, but its claim on the new year’s capacity had been treated as fixed background rather than as a choice.

Managers began stretching the same specialists across both commitments. The new priority’s first milestone slipped as specialist reviews that should have happened early were pushed behind remediation work. Meetings multiplied, decisions slowed, and work that looked fully staffed on paper started moving in fragments.

The pressure spread beyond those specialists. Project leads started moving milestones to fit the people they could get, finance held back some spending because dependent work couldn’t start, and senior leaders spent more time resolving clashes between commitments they believed had already been reconciled during planning.

The interesting thing was that the approved plan hadn’t changed, but the amount of work that could move at the same time already had.

The new initiative hadn’t been badly prioritized at all. The leadership team had already removed a lower-ranked proposal, but part of the capacity used in the ranking exercise simply hadn’t been available to begin with.

This is where the “Hidden Problems” execution leak appears.

The planning process had surfaced the remediation program, its budget and its expected completion date, yet the new work was still being ranked against an overstated view of what remained available.

A baseline records what’s already in motion, but it doesn’t force old work to justify its capacity against new work. Once carryover is treated as given, only the new initiatives are asked to compete.

That distinction matters because visibility can create false confidence.

Leaders can see every major piece of work on one page and still never face the question of whether an old commitment deserves to keep the people and budget it carried across the year boundary.

Listing carryover isn’t the same as choosing it again. The planning process therefore becomes disciplined about one side of the load while leaving the other side untouched.

When execution starts slowly, leadership tightens prioritization. Leaders ask for fewer initiatives, sharper business cases and clearer ranking, then delay or reject new proposals that can’t justify scarce capacity.

Those actions improve the choices among new priorities; however, they don’t reopen the older commitments already sitting in the baseline. That was the pattern in this business unit.

Leadership had reduced the new-priority list before approving the plan, and when capacity pressure appeared, the first response was to ask whether one of the new initiatives should move more slowly.

The remediation program wasn’t part of that debate because it had been approved in the prior year, and finishing it was treated as an “obligation” rather than as a competing use of scarce capacity.

The organization was re-ranking new work while the carryover never faced the same test.

A stronger planning process adds a formal carryover line. That certainly improves visibility, but it doesn’t change the underlying mechanism when carryover remains exempt from comparison.

The remediation work can appear clearly in the plan, with its budget, owner and expected completion date, and still never face the one central question: Is finishing this work now more valuable than starting the new priority that needs the same people?

In this business unit, the remediation program remained on every planning view. Its existence was never hidden. What did stay hidden was the effect of treating its capacity claim as “non-negotiable” while the new priorities competed for whatever was left.

The plan could be complete as an inventory and incomplete as a capacity decision.

Every item appeared somewhere, but not every item had to earn its place in the same contest for scarce people and budget.

By the time the conflict became obvious, leaders were dealing with a problem the planning process had already created. The remediation work couldn’t simply stop, and the new priority had already been approved.

The same scarce specialists now sat between two legitimate commitments, each with consequences for delay. Leaders were forced to make the tradeoff during execution instead of during planning, when they still had more room to change the portfolio.

When that conflict reached the next leadership review, the discussion was no longer about which work deserved to start. It was about which already-approved commitment would lose access to people both sides now depended on.

The plan didn’t fail because leaders chose the wrong new priorities. Not at all. The planning choice had been postponed until both commitments were already in motion.

A large business unit was entering its annual planning cycle with three new priorities competing for specialist capacity. The leadership team had already reduced the list once, and the remaining proposals had strong business cases, clear owners and estimated resource needs.

The planning baseline also showed an older regulatory-remediation program that would continue into the new year. Nobody had forgotten it. The work was visible, funded and already staffed because the program had missed its original completion date.

During the planning session, one executive asked whether the remediation program would release its specialists early enough for the new priorities to start as planned. The program lead said the current end date still held unless the final regulatory review produced additional work. The room accepted that date and returned to ranking the new priorities, treating the remediation capacity as already committed until then.

#5377. Sephora’s U.S. CEO initially turned down an entry-level job at the company because she could only wear black, white, or gray to the office

In 1998, Artemis Patrick turned down a job at a relatively small perfume brand that had just been acquired by the luxury giant LVMH. That company was Sephora, and 26 years later, she became its North America CEO. Patrick stepped into the top job for the global beauty retailer’s North America division in April 2024, earning a shoutout in its parent company’s half-year earnings call in July for “good performance.”But Patrick’s journey to the top of the cosmetics empire started with a detour into cigarettes.

Patrick was studying for her MBA at San Francisco State University when a friend introduced her to the LVMH brand, which was hiring for entry-level planning roles. Patrick initially went in to interview for a role at the duty-free giant DFS in the only category that was hiring: tobacco.

“I thought, oh my gosh, what am I going to be peddling cigarettes?” Patrick told the “How Leaders Lead” podcast in a recent episode. “This is crazy. So I [asked] if they had anything else, and she said, well there is this company called Sephora—LVMH just acquired it—and it sells fragrance.”

“Same salary, same building, because at the time Sephora was sharing the office floor with DFS. And I said, I mean, obviously I’ll take the beauty job. She said there’s only one catch: You have to wear black white, or gray.”

“And I said, I’ll take the cigarette job.”

Patrick, who emigrated to the U.S. from Iran at the age of 7, said her decision to take the DFS role rather than the beauty job wasn’t necessarily down to independence but rather to personal finances. After all, Patrick was a student, and her wardrobe was full of patterned dresses—she couldn’t afford to repurchase multiple monochromatic looks.

DFS turned out to be an “incredible opportunity” that took Patrick around the world and quickly propelled her from the cigarette category into wine. But in 2006, Sephora came calling again courtesy of a referral from Carolyn Bojanowski, now Sephora’s executive vice president for merchandising.

Patrick interviewed with the same HR representative she had turned down years before, and the corporate dress code of black, white, and gray (“concept colors,” as they were referred to at the time) was still in place.

“They’d added red to the concept at that point,” Patrick recalls. “It was actually another, I think, six or seven years before we added color.”

Patrick’s path to Sephora and then up its ranks wasn’t linear—after DFS she worked at Restoration Hardware and Peet’s Coffee & Tea—and said this diversity of experience is now precisely what she looks for when building her own teams.

“I feel that my job is to remove obstacles and to make sure that they get to do what we hired them to do,” added Patrick. “So I definitely believe in building diverse teams, and I do feel that my job as a leader is to protect them from the noise and deal with the things that I should be dealing with.”

Eleanor Pringle is an award-winning senior reporter at Fortune covering news, the economy, and personal finance. Eleanor previously worked as a business correspondent and news editor in regional news in the U.K. She completed her journalism training with the Press Association after earning a degree from the University of East Anglia.

#5376. Reddit’s stock has taken a battering this year, but its COO says it’s barely started banking ‘over a decade of karma’ from devoted users

Reddit boasts engagement metrics that would be the envy of many other online platforms: Over 80% of its monetization comes from loyal, logged-in users, who spend eight times as much time on the site in their fifth year as they did in their first.And yet, Reddit’s share price is down 62% for the year to date, as the platform grapples with an internet increasingly shaped by AI.In its Q3 earnings call in October, Reddit’s CEO, Steve Huffman, said Google’s AI Overviews and AI Mode were leading to a decline in search referrals to the site, the lifeblood of many social and media-adjacent businesses. The market did not like the implications, and the share price dropped from just shy of $130 apiece to a little under $91 overnight.

Chief Operating Officer Jen Wong told Fortune in an exclusive interview that some factors were lost in translation. The shifting relationship between Reddit and search engines “requires a different kind of partnership,” she said, rather than any separation. If anything, Wong believes Reddit is well-positioned to navigate the new era of online information gathering.

In their first year on Reddit, users tend to spend five minutes a day on the app or website. By their fifth year, that figure rises to 40 minutes, Wong tells Fortune. The number of “communities” (topic-focused discussion groups) that users are in jumps from 10 in the first year to more than 100 by their fifth.

“Reddit is really interesting because we have users who have over a decade of karma,” Wong said. “Reddit typically gets you as a young adult, and then you season over time in this incredible way. If you look at the chart, it’s very consistent.”

Wong sees users’ changing life stages reflected in the communities they join: “[They’ve] gone through life with Reddit. You started as a student, you got your first rental place, you got married, you had kids, and we see kind of your life’s journey.

“You just never age out of Reddit because all of those life stages are available to you on Reddit, and you’re always going through something that you have to traverse.”

Navigating different life stages appears to be a key differentiator of the Reddit platform. In 2024, an article published in “Higher Education Research and Development” found that one in three students use Reddit for study help, ahead of TikTok at 14.9% and Instagram at 12.7%. YouTube leads the pack, with more than 90% of the 1,000 students surveyed using it for educational purposes.

The site’s leadership wants to expand on that function. In early November, Reddit launched Reddit Reviews, organizing product feedback across multiple communities to provide overall ratings.

“Logged-in users season very, very well, which is another motivation for us to say we want more logged-in users, because we want the opportunity to teach you about all these other aspects of Reddit,” Wong adds, “Not just the information and retrieval part of Reddit, but the part of Reddit that is around the connection, the communities, and the conversation.”

Every media platform needs to maintain or grow its audience. But Reddit has a unique problem: It has more than 100,000 “communities,” according to various reports, all of which have volunteer moderators. These moderators are unpaid and are not Reddit employees, instead choosing to spend their free time building their communities and ensuring the content is fit for its purpose.

But with ever-evolving channels and new voices within them, demand for experienced moderators is high—in fact, Reddit even has a dedicated page where communities can recruit volunteer moderators.

In the recruitment group, individuals are either looking for or offering moderation skills for hours a day, on a daily basis. Posts include requests for moderators in specific time zones, often for about 3 hours a day.

But Wong says even if Reddit wanted to bring its moderators in-house and pay them, they probably wouldn’t take it. While moderators are interested in earning, she said, they didn’t want strings attached: “They really like their independence from us, to be able to say, ‘This is our community, we set the rules, and this is how we want to operate.’

“Our relationship with moderators, I think, has greatly improved. I’ve been with Reddit eight, almost nine years, and where at the beginning we were not investing as much as we could in creating moderator tools and making their lives better in terms of reducing some of the repetitive work, over the last few years we’ve done a much better job also applying AI to help them with a toolkit, so that they can spend the time on the things that they really care about.”

But overall, Wong is bullish on Reddit’s long-term position in the age of AI. “Reddit is basically the taste layer of the internet. No model and no recommendation system can be good, I think, without a dash of Reddit in it, because you just don’t have the freshness of information. That adds value in so many places.”

Eleanor Pringle is an award-winning senior reporter at Fortune covering news, the economy, and personal finance. Eleanor previously worked as a business correspondent and news editor in regional news in the U.K. She completed her journalism training with the Press Association after earning a degree from the University of East Anglia.

#5375. I Paid My Team a Bonus for Doing More — and the Work Got Worse. Here’s What It Taught Me.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

I paid my team a cash bonus for hitting a video target. Complaints rose, and cancellations hit 13%. Here is what the data showed and what fixed it.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

The bonus was simple. Hit a set number of completed videos and earn extra cash on top of your salary. I wanted more productivity, and a clear target seemed like the fairest way to ask for it.

After it started, creative quality dropped. At least a quarter of our clients began to complain, and our cancellation rate hit 13%.

The target said completed videos, so that is what it measured. Creative quality is harder to count. A cut that lands with the audience, a pause that gives a line room to breathe, a graphic that fits the story — none of those shows up in a tally. When one thing is counted, and the other isn’t, people look after the counted thing. That isn’t laziness. It’s what the plan asked for.

I paid extra for the thing I measured and lost the thing I valued. The clients noticed before I did.

For a while, we were clueless about what was happening. Then we dug into the revision requests. The revision rounds behind the complaints could easily have been avoided in the first edit.

We traced it further. Editors were bypassing parts of the process to save time. Where a video clearly needed motion graphics, they used basic B-roll instead. They also put less effort into building a stronger hook.

When we tracked mistakes by team and by editor, the same people were making the same mistakes on repeat. Those were the editors producing the most videos. New editors made repeat mistakes too, but they produced few videos, so that was a different problem.

That changed how I read the bonus. My read is that it paid people to skip the steps that protect quality.

I wasn’t the first owner to run into this. In a field experiment in Chinese factories, economists paid workers a bonus for output. Quantity rose, and quality fell sharply — and the effect was much stronger for workers on a flat wage. My editors are on fixed salaries, so I was in exactly that group.

A second study, published in Management Science, tested 224 retail stores. Regular performance review conversations raised profits by about 7%. A profit bonus alone produced no significant gain. Paying the bonus on top of the reviews erased the benefit of the reviews, and the authors’ surveys suggest the bonus changed the nature of the conversations.

Bonuses aren’t always the wrong tool. A research review by Dirk Sliwka for IZA World of Labor notes that they can work when the key tasks are easy to measure, and workers can change their output, as with installing windshields. A good edit isn’t easy to measure. None of this research comes from creative work, so I treat it as a pattern and not as proof for my business.

We stopped chasing volume. Editors who were doing good work got raises, and everyone else got a clear path to follow. Use the same steps, avoid revision rounds, and you qualify for a raise. A raise replaced the bonus.

The results came quickly. Within a month, our cancellation rate was back to single digits. For the next few months, we delivered better, and client retention went up. Our cancellation rate is now about 3%, which is normal. Clients pause or leave when they stop wanting to create content or have health or travel reasons. When we track why clients cancel, quality-related reasons are under 1.8%.

The difference is what each pays for. A volume bonus pays for finishing. A raise tied to fewer revisions pays for getting it right the first time, and it doesn’t disappear next month.

We’re also piloting a second model with three editors. They have a low base salary, and their pay grows with the clients they keep. Lose a client, and the commission drops. Keep one, and it grows, and a high-paying client can mean steady, high commission. Pay follows retention instead of volume, which makes each editor responsible for keeping their clients.

The early signal is small. The three editors are taking ownership of their clients because keeping them keeps their commission high. I’m seeing slightly better results so far. I won’t pretend that’s proof. Three people is a pilot, not a verdict.

While the pilot runs, we’re writing SOPs that define what quality work really means and how to track it. We also built a two-layer QC process, one AI layer and one human layer, so mistakes get caught before the client sees them.

The hard part hasn’t been the formula. It’s been the people. Most of the team still wants fixed income for peace of mind, and I understand why. A low base with a bigger upside asks someone to take on risk they never signed up for. A few editors are willing to try but want certainty about what they’ll earn. I don’t have a clean answer yet.

Before you add a bonus, here are the questions I would ask now: What am I counting, and what matters that I am not counting? Am I tracking rework next to output? It was the only way we found who was skipping steps. Can the person actually change the number? And what will they do if the only way to hit it is to cut a corner?

If you change how people are paid, pilot it with volunteers and expect resistance. A pay change is a change to the deal.

The bonus was simple. Hit a set number of completed videos and earn extra cash on top of your salary. I wanted more productivity, and a clear target seemed like the fairest way to ask for it.

After it started, creative quality dropped. At least a quarter of our clients began to complain, and our cancellation rate hit 13%.

The target said completed videos, so that is what it measured. Creative quality is harder to count. A cut that lands with the audience, a pause that gives a line room to breathe, a graphic that fits the story — none of those shows up in a tally. When one thing is counted, and the other isn’t, people look after the counted thing. That isn’t laziness. It’s what the plan asked for.

#5373. Why hiring neurodivergent talent isn’t enough, and what leaders should do instead

Many neuroinclusion strategies still depend on employees disclosing a diagnosis. Jonathan Mok argues support should be built into how organizations operate.

This article has been reviewed by the Quartz editorial team. The content may be licensed for reuse.

Companies are increasingly recognizing the value of neurodivergent talent, but hiring is only part of the picture. Many neuroinclusion strategies still rely on employees to disclose their diagnoses and request workplace adjustments themselves, an approach that assumes they feel safe doing so. According to a 2026 survey by the nonprofit Understood.org, about 70% of neurodivergent employees in the U.S. worry that disclosing their neurodivergence could negatively affect them at work. When employees stay silent, employers may never learn which barriers need addressing.

Jonathan Mok, a Hong Kong-based neurodiversity advocate, speaker, and leadership trainer, has seen that gap from both sides. He was diagnosed with ADHD and autism at 37, after years of working in education in Hong Kong. Today, he trains corporate teams across Asia on neuroinclusion and coaches executives who have received late diagnoses. His own experience suggests that even when employees do disclose, formal support does not always translate into belonging.

Jonathan Mok, neurodiversity advocate, speaker, and leadership trainer.

After his diagnosis, a workplace medical committee recommended that Mok should not feel obliged to attend department social gatherings. When his boss invited the team to a New Year lunch and he raised his hand to join, colleagues kept telling him nobody was forcing him to go. They meant well, but a measure intended to protect him left him feeling excluded. “I wanted to go. My boss was paying for lunch,” Mok recalls. “But the message I kept hearing was that I didn’t really belong there.”

Despite receiving formal accommodations, Mok continued to face challenges at work, and he resigned in 2020. His experience reflects a wider pattern. In a 2025 report by Boston Consulting Group, supported by SG Enable, 62% of neurodivergent employees surveyed in Singapore said their neurodivergence had been misunderstood as a poor attitude. While 99% believed reasonable accommodations would help, only 33% said these were available at their workplace, and just 24% considered them adequate.

The findings point to a disconnect between recognizing neurodivergent talent and creating the conditions for it to thrive. Gartner predicted in 2023 that by 2027, a quarter of Fortune 500 companies would actively recruit neurodivergent talent to improve business performance. Recruitment, however, is only the first step. Inclusion also depends on whether employees feel they belong, can speak up without fear of judgment, and receive support that works in practice.

Mok believes that an emphasis on meritocracy can lead some employers to assume that anyone capable enough to be hired does not need to disclose anything. Employees, in turn, try to fit in until they no longer can. He adds that organizations often focus on deficits and rely heavily on medical guidance rather than on what individuals actually want or need. In his view, support should not depend on employees asking for it; it should be built into how the organization operates.

He also challenges the idea that organizations must be ready to hire neurodivergent employees before taking any steps toward inclusion. One cosmetics retailer found that quiet shopping hours did little to ease the sensory demands of a busy store. After consulting Mok, a colleague, and store staff, it introduced ribbon-marked baskets that let customers signal a preference for minimal interaction without explaining their needs. Because retail turnover is high, the accompanying staff training was kept simple enough to pass on to new employees.

Mok points to a neurodivergent internship program at the Hong Kong office of an international insurer as a more comprehensive example. Rather than treating recruitment as the endpoint, the company paired the program with manager training and structured onboarding, helping teams build the skills to support neurodivergent colleagues. It also works with a local nonprofit organization to source talent and provide training.

To help organizations turn good intentions into action, Mok uses a 4P framework covering People, Place, Policy, and Program. It is designed as an ongoing approach rather than a one-time training session. Under People, he encourages organizations to recognize inclusive managers, create safe channels for raising concerns, and highlight neurodivergent role models. Under Place, he recommends sensory-friendly workspaces and normalizing tools that allow people to work in ways that suit them.

Policy involves clear procedures around disclosure, workplace adjustments, and job expectations, so that employees and managers know what support is available. Many managers, Mok notes, only look for guidance after a problem arises and then have to dig through documents that can run 50 or 60 pages. The program focuses on long-term planning, consultation, and partnerships with community organizations, including neurodivergent individuals and their families, so that initiatives address real needs rather than assumptions.

For companies operating across Asia, Mok stresses the importance of understanding how culture, law, and local knowledge shape neurodiversity in each market. Even within the region, conditions such as autism and ADHD are recognized differently, as the contrast between Hong Kong and mainland China shows. Such differences can complicate standardized inclusion policies. He also believes that meaningful progress is possible for organizations of every size, not only multinational corporations.

For Mok, the next stage of neuroinclusion means looking past whether organizations are willing to hire neurodivergent people and asking whether their cultures, policies, and leadership allow those employees to stay and succeed. “The next diversity metric should not be hires,” he says. “It should be stays.” A seat at the New Year lunch, offered without hesitation, may say more about an organization’s inclusion than any recruitment target.

#5372. ‘An epic fail’: Crypto world blasts Netflix’s ‘The Altruists’ for turning SBF’s crimes into a love story

A new Netflix series that tells the story of crypto crook Sam Bankman-Fried is winning decent reviews from TV critics and the public. But not everyone is a fan. People familiar with the crypto industry are taking to social media to blast the makers of “The Altruists” for distorting the nature of Bankman-Fried’s relationship with one-time girlfriend, Caroline Ellison, and for depicting the convicted felons as misguided idealists. The series, which dropped last week, is also taking fire for suggesting without evidence that Binance founder Changpeng Zhao is the real villain of the story—a depiction some claim is rooted in anti-Chinese racism.

The 8-part series, which lists Barack and Michelle Obama as executive producers, is based on real-world events that led to the 2022 collapse of Bankman-Fried’s crypto exchange, FTX. A subsequent FBI investigation resulted in Ellison pleading guilty and testifying against her former boyfriend, who is currently serving 25 years in federal prison for defrauding customers of billions of dollars.

Filmmakers regularly take liberties in order to increase dramatic impact. In the case of “The Altruists”, though, critics say the series engages in outright falsehoods by minimizing Bankman-Fried’s crimes, and depicting him as a victim who acted under duress from Binance’s Zhao. Don Wilson, the CEO of the crypto market-making firm DRW, posted a widely-shared clip from The Altruists showing Zhao and Bankman-Fried on X, describing it as “preposterous” and “an epic fail.”

This is an epic fail by Netflix. Recasting this as something @SBF_FTX and Caroline were forced to do in order to placate @cz_binance – instead of highlighting the effective altruist ethos that drove them to commit yet another crime is preposterous. https://t.co/bV6IsoG6mE

The clip itself shows Zhao’s character telling Ellison and Bankman-Fried that FTX is failing to grow fast enough to justify an early investment he made in the exchange, and declaring that he will financially destroy the exchange if the pair fail to collude with him in a criminal trading scheme.

While Zhao was indeed an early investor in FTX, the issue of coercion never came up at Bankman-Fried’s criminal trial, and there is no evidence the exchange depicted in the clip ever took place. Another crypto industry vet on X likewise objected to another scene for “making SBF and Caroline look like innocent victims who were bullied” by Zhao.

Netflix portrayed @cz_binance as a complete moron in its new FTX movie while making SBF and Caroline look like innocent victims who were bullied.Who the hell wrote this script? pic.twitter.com/HjAwQ3N3W9

Others objected to the heavy Cantonese accent affected by Zhao’s character, played by Terry Chen, complaining it promoted stereotypes. Zhao himself wrote on X, “hmm… I grew up in Canada, worked in the New York, Tokyo, many places. I almost never felt being targeted by racism. But something to think about…”. Veteran crypto journalist Laura Shin expressed a similar sentiment, stating “I’m just going to say it: Racism has to have played a role in how they portrayed [Zhao]. There’s no other explanation.”

Aside from the depictions of Zhao, other viewers complained that “The Altruists” wrongly portrayed Ellison as the mastermind behind a series of accounting frauds used to conceal holes in the balance sheet of FTX and of Bankman-Fried’s hedge fund, Alameda Research. This contradicts contemporary news accounts and evidence from the criminal trial, which unambiguously pointed to Bankman-Fried as the one responsible for a series of frauds.

Those weighing in to complain about the depictions included FTX’s former COO, Constance Wang, who wrote, “Maybe you’ll enjoy The Altruists as a romantic comedy. For those of us who watched it together, it felt like someone else’s story with our names attached.”

Meanwhile, some critics of “The Altruists” suggested that the numerous inaccuracies could be explained in part for political reasons. Lawyer Hailey Lennon pointed to the production’s ties to the Obamas and Bankman-Fried’s hefty donations to the Democratic party, writing “The framing of the movie as some love story and to make SBF look more innocent is even more calculated than I initially realized. Always follow the money.”

The Altruists was produced by Michelle and Barak Obama SBF publicly donated $39.8 million to Democratic candidates and aligned outside groups during the 2021–2022 election cycleThe framing of the movie as some love story and to make SBF look more innocent is even more… pic.twitter.com/pzvWJP7tUH

Others on social media likewise pointed to the Obamas’ involvement, and Bankman-Fried’s donations to the Democratic party—including $5.2 million to former President Joe Biden’s campaign—as an explanation for the film’s depictions.

Bankman-Fried, who remains incarcerated in federal prison in California, has failed to express remorse for stealing over $8 billion from FTX customers and investors. He is currently slated to be released around 2047.

Jeff John Roberts is the Finance and Crypto editor at Fortune, overseeing coverage of the blockchain and how technology is changing finance.

#5371. Small businesses drive the economy. Who is financing their growth?

Small businesses drive much of U.S. job growth but often struggle to qualify for bank loans. Colin Kilgour sees an opening for private credit.

This article has been reviewed by the Quartz editorial team. The content may be licensed for reuse.

When a business looks to expand its operations or invest in new equipment, its growth often depends on access to the right financing. Across America, the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that from 2013 to 2023, small businesses contributed 55% of the country’s total net job creation. Between March 2023 and March 2024, they accounted for 88.9% of net job growth, according to the U.S. Small Business Administration’s Office of Advocacy. These figures highlight the important role small businesses play in supporting the economy. Yet, these small businesses that increasingly help the economy grow are the ones still struggling to get the support that they need.

According to a report released by the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, small businesses account for between 43.5% and 50.7% of U.S. GDP and generated nearly $5.9 trillion in 2014, the most recent year available. This further illustrates how essential small businesses are to the broader economy of America. However, their economic importance may not always translate to easier access to financial opportunities.

Traditionally, one of the main barriers to small business lending is the regulatory requirements that govern how banks allocate their lending capital. Different types of loans carry different risks. Small businesses may be at a disadvantage, since their loans generally carry higher regulatory risk ratings than other forms of lending.

Collateral is another challenge. Many small businesses may not be equipped with the collateral banks typically require, such as commercial property, expensive equipment, or outstanding receivables. Processing these loans can also be costly. Since smaller loans often generate less revenue but require almost the same amount of work as larger loans, banks may find them less profitable to offer.

For Colin Kilgour, co-founder and principal of Kilgour Williams Capital, these challenges present an opportunity for investors within the private credit market. Through his work in credit and structured finance, Kilgour has seen how traditional lending practices can leave many small businesses neglected and disregarded.

Colin Kilgour, co-founder and principal of Kilgour Williams Capital.

He views the main challenge as helping small businesses secure the funding they need. “Many businesses need money to expand, renovate, or grow their operations, but struggle to qualify for traditional bank loans,” he says. He adds that some do not have the assets banks require as security, while others need smaller loans that banks may be less willing to provide.

Kilgour identifies these barriers as an opportunity for private credit to serve businesses that are often overlooked. He noted that relying solely on conventional lending requirements ought to be reconsidered. Private credit providers can look into assessing the business’s cash flow and ability to repay. Overall, his view is to offer another perspective that creates a potential source of financing for business owners who need capital to support their growth.

“Technology has changed how these businesses can be assessed,” he says. Kilgour points to open banking, which allows lenders to review a business’s financial activity. Modern financial technology, in addition, makes it possible to evaluate records and inspect business operations remotely. He emphasizes that technological advancement allows lenders to assess a business’s financial position remotely and more easily. These tools can help lenders make faster and more informed lending decisions.

In Kilgour’s view, loans can help fund expansion, equipment, or renovations while allowing owners to retain control of their businesses. The opportunity, however, also comes with risks. He recognizes that small businesses do not carry the same credit profiles as larger, investment-grade companies, which means lenders must account for potential losses and build diversified portfolios.

Kilgour sees these challenges as part of why the small-business private credit market still has room to grow. He believes the market may expand significantly as more business owners become aware of financing options beyond traditional banks. For him, the opportunity is not limited to large companies or major transactions. It may also lie in supporting the smaller businesses that contribute to the wider economy but have historically had fewer financing options.

“Private credit connects businesses with needed capital while opening opportunities for investors in an underserved market,” he says. In his view, investors should look beyond large corporate lending to Main Street businesses. By assessing risk carefully and finding more effective ways to provide capital, private credit can help connect underserved businesses with the financing they need to grow.

#5369. Global stocks move upward despite shock warning from Panmure Liberum analyst who sold all equities in his personal portfolio

With America offline for Thanksgiving, the rest of the world enjoyed a break from the market chaos caused by U.S. tariff policy, U.S. AI investment, and U.S. interest rate rises. In Asia, stocks broadly rose. Europe was up strongly. And although New York was closed for the holiday, S&P 500 futures were up.Nasdaq 100 futures were up 0.63%, and Nvidia was up 1.29% in after-market trading.None of this should be happening!

There is nothing but bad news on the horizon, multiple Wall Street and London City analysts said in emails to Fortune.

The most dramatic warning came from Panmure Liberum’s Joachim Klement (who writes a well-regarded Substack on investing whose subtitle is “Thoughts on financial markets by a grumpy, middle-aged German. What more do you want?”)

He gave a video talk in which he announced he was selling all the equities—all of them!—in his personal investment portfolio because of the recent selloff in the S&P 500: “I think that we are heading towards a major bear market with more than 30% drawdown risk.” His official forecast for 2027 is that the S&P 500 will sink to 5,000—a level that right now seems unthinkable. His concern is that the index is currently trading below its 200-day moving average: “As Paul Tudor Jones the famous investor once said, nothing good happens below the 200-day moving average.”

Firstly, inflation is still too high. The Fed’s preferred metric, the index for personal consumption expenditures, was up year-over-year to 3.8% in October, up from 3.7% the month before. “Undesirably strong,” as Lawrence Werther and Brendan Stuart of Daiwa Capital Markets said in a note. That will almost certainly push the Fed into raising interest rates in December in order to make money more scarce—a scenario that generally augurs poorly for stocks.

Many analysts pointed to a speech given Monday by John Williams, the President of the New York Fed. He all but telegraphed that the Fed was going to kick the rate up soon: “We must take actions over time that will ensure that we get inflation back to our 2 percent goal in a timely manner and on a sustained basis. There is still work to do to get that done.” (There is a good analysis of the speech by economist Claudia Sahm here.)

Secondly, the U.S. economy is strong, so the Fed will feel it has the breathing space to dampen inflationary demand.

New jobless claims came in near their three-year low, and the long-term trend in jobless claims continues to point down, according to Thomas Simons and Blake Birkins of Jefferies.

“The big highlight … is GDP, which at 4.3% shows that the economy is booming, but unfortunately the inflation data is still too high and is unlikely to convince the Fed to remain on hold,” Chris Zaccarelli, chief investment officer at Northlight Asset Management, told Fortune via email.

“Between the AI angst and the newly announced tariffs, it doesn’t look like the Santa Claus rally is in store for us this year,” he said.

Although U.S. stocks may be sliding, that’s mostly because the tech sector is a fiasco right now. Outside the tech sector (and the outperformance of European stocks vs U.S. stocks is a good example of this), things are going rather well. Before the turkey holiday, 372 stocks in the S&P 500 moved higher, and the equal-weight index was up 0.82% on the day, Deutsche Bank’s Jim Reid noticed.

Jim Edwards is the executive editor for global news at Fortune. He was previously the editor-in-chief of Business Insider's news division and the founding editor of Business Insider UK. His investigative journalism has changed the law in two U.S. federal districts and two states. The U.S. Supreme Court cited his work on the death penalty in the concurrence to Baze v. #5367. Hurt By Inflation? Here Are 13 Real-World Ways To Cut Costs In Your Business

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

With inflation still running hot, these simple moves can trim your business costs without slowing you down.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Inflation remains stubborn. Producer prices are now running at a 6.5% annual clip, and affordability is top of mind. Want to cut some costs in your business? Of course you do.  Try these moves.

Both ChatGPT and Claude offer connections to your bank account and credit card services. Or, if you’re nervous about that, just upload your statements.  You’ll be impressed by the number of suggestions they make to reduce your spending and better manage expenses.

I used to think canceling online subscriptions would be a big headache, and years ago it was. Not anymore. Search for “cancel my subscription on Google Play” (or Apple or Amazon), and you’ll get direct links to do it. I’m betting you and your business have subscriptions you’ve forgotten about that are eating up hundreds of dollars a year.

Every year, put your business and auto insurance policies out for a quote. Ask your AI chatbot to make suggestions too. This is not very time-consuming and can be accomplished using an administrative person in your office. We’re oftentimes too lazy to do this.  And that’s costing us.

Many of my clients have complicated, expensive coffee machines in their break rooms with a wide variety of coffees. They also stock sugar packets, teas, mini creamers, plastic stirrers and paper cups. It’s too much. Offer fewer coffees so you order less. Put out a sugar bowl, bring in a gallon of creamer and go back to ceramic mugs. Call me Scrooge, but it saves money.

NerdWallet does a great job regularly reviewing business and personal credit cards. Again, use your AI chatbot to look at your spending and tell it your preferences and you’ll get plenty of recommendations too.  Moving to a better card could earn you more points and cashback rewards then you’re getting right now. I have some clients that regularly switch back and forth.

Speaking of credit, if your business buys products on Amazon, then make sure you use one of Amazon’s credit cards for purchases.  With a Prime membership, you can earn 5% back on eligible Amazon purchases, and there’s no annual fee.

If you can’t pay off a credit card purchase right away from operations, consider using working capital or a lower-rate loan to reduce the balance. Credit card interest rates are high, so this can cut what you pay in interest significantly.

This is a very common tax move, yet so many of us ignore it. Put as much as you can into your retirement plan to lower your tax bill this year.  When you save – assuming you’re eligible – sock money into a Roth IRA or Roth 401K so your after-tax money grows tax-free.  With a Roth, there are no minimum distributions, and you can take the money out whenever you want, provided it meets certain requirements like a first-time home purchase, higher education or unreimbursed medical expenses.

Make sure your company has an HSA and contribute the max. It will reduce your tax expense and allow you to save money for future healthcare expenses.

Every square foot your inventory takes up costs you in overhead and space. Twice a year, take a hard look at your inventory and get rid of what isn’t moving. Sell it on Craigslist, eBay or Facebook Marketplace or scrap it.

Mark Cuban’s Cost Plus Drugs and Amazon Pharmacy both offer options that let businesses provide discounted prescription drugs, and they work with many popular health plans.

Set up a donor-advised fund and contribute to it this year, even if you haven’t decided which charities or nonprofits will receive the money. You take the deduction now and choose the recipients later.

I like Capital One Shopping. Add it as a browser extension for yourself and anyone else who makes purchases for your business. Whenever someone is on a shopping site, it searches for available coupons before you buy. It works about half the time, and it has saved me significant money over the years.

We can all afford the things we want — it’s just that sometimes we choose to spend our money on other things instead. That’s fine. But know that cutting back on things like travel, entertainment, subscriptions, marketing or other discretionary spending in your business (and your personal life) can help you reallocate your cash for other purposes.  You’re more in control than you think.

#5366. ‘Sister isn’t free’: Melinda French Gates fact-checks viral ‘SNL’ sketch on eldercare

Geek Life: Fun stories, memes, humor and other random items at the intersection of tech, science, business and culture.  SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 18, 2026 at 1:23 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 1:23 pm

A “Saturday Night Live” skit about caring for aging relatives touched a viral nerve after it aired over the weekend, including with Melinda French Gates, who offered her own “fact check” on the too-close-to-home comedy.

The sketch, a fake commercial, stars host John Mulaney as a man who has found an easy way to care for his aging father without upending his own life: “Sister,” an “elder care system” that is free and is, in fact, his sister.

French Gates wrote on Instagram this week that the sketch “is funny because it’s a little too true.” Using research from Pivotal, her investment and philanthropic organization, she went through the ad’s claims one by one and found that most held up:

Sister will provide. True, French Gates said, citing AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving. Among adults ages 55 to 64, women are nearly 40% more likely than men to care for an older relative, and nearly 40% more likely to provide constant care.

She’ll quit her job. “Mostly true,” at least the job part. Catalyst found that 42% of women who voluntarily left jobs in 2025 cited caregiving as the main reason.

Paid help is pricey. “True, unfortunately.” New America puts the average home health aide at more than $6,600 a month, and 24-hour care can top $25,000.

Sister may break down. Also true. In the Caregiving in the U.S. 2025 report, nearly two-thirds of caregivers said they were under moderate or high emotional stress, and women felt the strain more than men did.

“Free” is misleading. French Gates said Sister isn’t free; she’s the one paying for the care, in lost wages, stalled careers, thinner retirement savings and less time for her own life.

French Gates has made women’s health and caregiving central to her work since she stepped down as co-chair of the Gates Foundation in 2024.

She left with $12.5 billion to put toward her work on behalf of women and families. Much of that work runs through Pivotal, the Seattle-area organization she founded to handle her philanthropy and investments. In June she pledged another $215 million for women’s health, which brought her giving in that area to more than $600 million over two years. The pledge included $10 million to the Menopause Society for better menopause care in the U.S.

The sketch has been shared widely across the country this week, in part because it lines up so closely with the research.

In its own analysis, The New York Times cited studies showing that daughters generally provide at least twice as much care to aging parents as sons do. The U.S., unlike many wealthy countries, offers no federal paid leave or long-term care insurance for family caregivers.

French Gates said she welcomed the conversation.

“I’m so glad we’re talking about this, and laughing about it,” she wrote on Instagram. “We need more honesty about what caring for loved ones really takes and why so much of that work falls to women. But I’d love for the day to come when these jokes don’t pack quite the same punch — because we’ve made it so much easier to care for the people we love.”

#5365. Google acquires Seattle startup Howie and its AI scheduling assistant

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 18, 2026 at 2:03 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 2:03 pm

Google is bringing Seattle-based Howie, maker of an AI scheduling assistant that works from your inbox, into its Google Labs division.

Terms of the deal were not disclosed this week. Google Labs, the company’s experimental arm, announced the acquisition in a post on X, saying it “can’t wait to learn from them as we build the next generation of intuitive AI tools together for small businesses.”

Howie CEO and co-founder Austin Petersmith said on LinkedIn that the team will continue building Howie at Google. “Howie has always been built on top of Gmail and Google Calendar, so Google Labs is the perfect place for us to take this product to the next level,” he wrote.

Petersmith co-founded Howie around 2023 with CTO Dave Newman. The two first worked together in 2013 at Assembly, which Newman co-founded, and prototyped an AI assistant in 2015 before deciding the market wasn’t ready.

We’re excited to welcome Howie to Google Labs! The @Howie_ai team has spent years figuring out scheduling and calendar management. We can’t wait to learn from them as we build the next generation of intuitive AI tools together for small businesses 🤝 https://t.co/8bzjebeGdD

Users cc Howie on an email thread, and it coordinates meeting times, adds events to calendars, follows up as needed and flags scheduling conflicts. Customers set their own rules in an open-ended preferences document, such as “if it’s a pitch call, set it to 25 minutes and use Zoom.”

Behind the scenes, Howie ran tasks through fine-tuned language models and looped in human scheduling experts when the AI wasn’t confident.

Howie raised a $6 million seed round led by True Ventures in September 2025, when it launched publicly out of private beta. At the time, it had more than 1,000 paying customers, including startup founders, venture capitalists, recruiters, consultants and journalists, and was scheduling more than 5,000 meetings a week.

The deal comes as Google and rivals including OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta race to build AI agents that complete tasks on behalf of users. Google Labs acquired music generation platform ProducerAI earlier this year.

#5364. Stop Using AI as an Excuse for Layoffs. Here’s How to Use AI to Retain Talent Instead

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

How to use AI to make your team more capable, not smaller.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

When a company announces layoffs and points to AI, I always want to know what happened first. Did the technology fundamentally change how work gets done, or did leadership already need to reduce costs and AI became a convenient explanation?

There is a meaningful difference. AI can automate tasks, accelerate workflows and change the skills a company needs. But AI does not walk into a boardroom and decide how many people should remain employed. Leaders decide what happens to the capacity the technology creates.

That distinction matters because employees are watching. If every AI announcement is followed by layoffs, people quickly learn that greater efficiency puts their jobs at risk and they have little reason to embrace the tools leadership wants them to use.

There is another way to implement AI. Start by asking how it can make your people more capable.

I learned this lesson long before the current AI boom. When we were building Amazon Web Services, talented engineers were spending too much time provisioning servers, configuring storage and handling infrastructure before they could get to the work they were actually there to do. By removing that friction, we gave developers more capacity to build, experiment and solve customer problems.

I saw the same principle years later with a junior attorney who spent hours researching and formatting before reaching the work that required her judgment. Generative AI could produce a first draft in minutes, giving her more time to refine the facts and shape the narrative for the client’s best outcome.

That is the opportunity leaders should look for with AI. Before calculating how many positions an efficiency gain could eliminate, ask what your people could accomplish if repetitive work stopped consuming so much of their day.

Suppose AI gives a team back 10 or 20% of its capacity. What happens to that time?

It could be the customer follow-up that keeps getting postponed, an improvement sitting in the backlog or a relationship that needs more attention. Those opportunities already exist inside most businesses. The problem is that people have been too busy with repetitive work to pursue them.

I saw this with a team of customer service agents who spent a significant portion of their day filling out forms and navigating cumbersome systems. An AI tool automated part of that process and gave them roughly an hour back each day.

Leadership could have used that hour to justify a smaller team. Instead, employees spent more time connecting with customers, strengthening relationships and solving more complex problems. AI removed work they disliked and created room for work where they could contribute more.

Retaining talent requires planning for people at the beginning of an AI initiative rather than after deployment. If leaders automate first and ask what happens to employees later, the priority is already clear.

Before introducing AI, divide the work into three categories. Some tasks contain little meaningful judgment and can be automated. Others can be accelerated by AI while still requiring human judgment. A third group should remain primarily human because relationships, creativity or judgment create the value. Then make the next decision before deploying anything. Where will the recovered capacity go?

That could mean moving people toward customer relationships, product development, higher-level analysis or other work that contributes more directly to growth. The destination will vary by organization, but leaders should know where they want people to go before technology begins changing their roles.

How you introduce AI also shapes whether employees embrace or resist it. If the first message people hear is that a tool will save 40% of their time, they may immediately wonder what leadership plans to do with that 40%.

Tell employees which frustrating work you want to reduce. Show them what they will have more time to accomplish. Explain how their roles can become more valuable as AI handles repetitive tasks.

Then demonstrate that commitment through what happens next. If employees see recovered time consistently reinvested into better work, stronger skills and new opportunities, AI starts to look like a tool they can use rather than a threat they need to survive.

Leaders can begin before buying another AI tool. Take one team and map how AI could change its work, then answer these four questions together before deployment.

1. What work should disappear? Break roles into individual tasks and identify repetitive work that consumes time without requiring significant human judgment. Focus first on removing friction rather than removing positions.

2. What human capability should grow? For every task AI can automate or accelerate, identify what employees could do with the recovered time. Look for work involving customers, relationships, creativity, problem-solving or judgment.

3. Where will the recovered capacity go? Give those hours a destination before deployment. If AI saves a team eight hours each week, decide whether those hours will go toward customer service, innovation, new revenue opportunities or another measurable priority.

4. What will you tell employees? Explain what AI will take off their plates and what you want them doing more of as a result. Managers should be able to describe that future clearly before asking employees to adopt the technology.

AI will change jobs, and some roles will change significantly as companies redesign how work gets done. But leaders still control a critical decision about what they do with the capacity AI creates.

Before treating efficiency as a reason to reduce headcount, ask what your people could accomplish with the time they get back. The companies that answer that question first have an opportunity to use AI for something far more valuable than cutting costs. They can use it to build a more capable workforce.

When a company announces layoffs and points to AI, I always want to know what happened first. Did the technology fundamentally change how work gets done, or did leadership already need to reduce costs and AI became a convenient explanation?

There is a meaningful difference. AI can automate tasks, accelerate workflows and change the skills a company needs. But AI does not walk into a boardroom and decide how many people should remain employed. Leaders decide what happens to the capacity the technology creates.

That distinction matters because employees are watching. If every AI announcement is followed by layoffs, people quickly learn that greater efficiency puts their jobs at risk and they have little reason to embrace the tools leadership wants them to use.

Zeno Power has hit a major milestone in its push to build nuclear batteries for underwater use.

The startup said today that it successfully demonstrated an electrically heated Stirling generator in a controlled maritime setting in Washington state. The two-week demonstration produced electrical power outputs in excess of 20 watts, said Lindsey Boles, Zeno’s chief product officer.

“It’s a really big step for us — just solidifying our expertise in how to design these, and then confirming our ability to translate that into operational hardware that meets or exceeds what our customers need,” Boles told GeekWire.

Zeno is developing the power system with support from the Department of Defense as a follow-up to an initial $7.5 million contract awarded in 2023. The generator uses a Stirling engine to convert heat into electricity by cycling gas through heating and cooling phases in a closed cylinder.

For the recent demonstration, the prototype device relied on an electric heating element. Future devices will instead rely on heat generated by the radioactive decay of strontium-90, a radioisotope that can be extracted from spent nuclear fuel.

Nuclear batteries have been in use for decades, primarily for space missions ranging from the Apollo moon shots to NASA’s Voyager spacecraft and Mars rovers. But the batteries being developed by Zeno Power promise to be at least four times more efficient than traditional radioisotope thermoelectric generators, Boles said.

Boles said the non-radiological test exceeded expectations. “There’s a difference between a design that works on paper and hardware that works in the field,” she said in a news release. “This is the moment our team has been building toward: proof that this technology works outside the lab.”

Long-lasting nuclear batteries could be used to power undersea sensor networks or recharge autonomous underwater vehicles. “There are a lot of applications, especially on the maritime front, that we really want electricity for,” Boles said. “And we really don’t need a ton of it. But we need it to be really reliable, and we need it to be long endurance, and we need it to be self-managed. … I think of it like a slow Tesla supercharger on the seabed.”

Retired Navy Adm. John Richardson, former chief of naval operations and a member of Zeno’s board of directors, called the recent test an “important step toward undersea superiority.”

“Protecting maritime infrastructure and powering distributed systems at sea requires energy; energy that lasts for years, not days or months,” Richardson said in a written statement. “As competition intensifies in contested domains, powered subsea systems will help keep us ahead. Zeno Power has steadily reduced risk, proven its technology, built a supply chain, and prepared to scale production.”

Next year, Zeno Power plans to install a radioisotope heat source in its generator and test the system in a water tank under controlled laboratory conditions. If those tests are successful, Zeno will move forward with the first operational seabed deployment of its radioisotope-fueled maritime system later in 2027.

The maritime battery isn’t Zeno’s only product. The company is also working on a nuclear-powered heater system for spacecraft, with a demonstration on the lunar surface planned as early as 2028. Zeno’s broader vision is to provide long-lasting, reliable power on the moon and Mars, and in extreme environments on Earth.

Since its founding in 2018, Zeno has secured $105 million in private capital and has brought in $60 million in contracts with the Pentagon and NASA. The company has more than 95 employees at locations in Seattle, California and Washington, D.C., with the largest contingent working at its engineering headquarters in Seattle’s South Lake Union district.

#5362. Amazon’s $18B bet on Anthropic tops $200B, for a moment, in the Claude maker’s historic market debut

by Todd Bishop on Nov 19, 2026 at 9:54 amNovember 19, 2026 at 10:10 am

Anthropic made its Nasdaq debut today in a record $81.3 billion initial public offering, with big financial stakes for the Seattle area’s two tech giants.

For Amazon, the IPO is a paper windfall. The company started putting money into Anthropic in 2023, about $18 billion in all. At the $83 IPO price, its stake was worth about $161 billion. With Anthropic opening at $111.50 a share, that number was closer to $216 billion. The stock has since dropped below $100, which put Amazon’s stake under $200 billion.

Beyond the value of the investment, Anthropic is a major customer for Amazon’s cloud platform. The Claude maker has committed to spend at least $110 billion on Amazon Web Services through 2036.

For Microsoft, it’s more complicated. The Redmond company agreed in late 2025 to invest up to $5 billion but hasn’t disclosed the size of its stake. Microsoft is buying $1 billion of Anthropic stock alongside the IPO, one of seven tech companies buying a combined $26 billion. Anthropic has committed to spend at least $47 billion on Microsoft’s Azure cloud through 2033.

But Microsoft is also pitching its own AI models against Anthropic’s, and it has been working to replace Anthropic’s models with OpenAI’s in some Copilot features, The Information reported this week.

Listing Anthropic’s compute partners on CNBC this morning, co-founder Daniela Amodei named Nvidia, Amazon, Google and Broadcom, but not Microsoft. Whether it was a slip or something more significant, it was an interesting omission.

A historic debut: The offering tops SpaceX’s $75 billion IPO in June, and it makes Anthropic the first standalone AI lab to go public, ahead of OpenAI.

The five-year-old company was valued at about $1.5 trillion at the $83 IPO price, on a fully diluted basis that counts employee stock and other shares not yet issued. The stock opened at $111.50, valuing Anthropic at about $2 trillion on the same basis. It has since traded as low as about $95.

Speaking before the opening bell, CEO Dario Amodei said Anthropic will slow the training and release of its AI models for as long as it takes to be confident they’re safe, and that going public only strengthens that resolve.

“We will not bend to either business nor political pressure,” he said.

In an interview with CNBC’s Andrew Ross Sorkin afterward, Amodei called the push and pull between growth and that kind of restraint “one of the central tensions at the heart of the company.”

Anthropic is also a public benefit corporation, a structure that legally requires the company to balance shareholders’ interests with the public good.

What’s next: Both Seattle-area giants have hedged their bets. Microsoft owns about 24% of OpenAI, and Amazon put $50 billion into OpenAI earlier this year.

OpenAI, which confidentially filed for its own IPO in June, is still aiming to go public in 2027.

Anthropic’s co-founders and some of its biggest shareholders are barred from selling for up to a year under the IPO’s lock-up rules, and Amazon has said it expects a customary lock-up period.

Amazon will update the value of its Anthropic holdings in its fourth-quarter results, much of it through earnings, which means the paper windfall is likely to boost Amazon’s fourth-quarter profit even though it hasn’t sold a share.

#5361. Should You Run Your Own AI or Pay a Provider? Here’s How to Decide.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Open-weight models finally give businesses a real choice between running AI on their own servers or renting it from the cloud.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

I’m an AI engineer and I’m currently building ChatMakr, an AI-powered platform that creates multi-agent chatbots in seconds, powered by open-weight models. I also spent time at a consulting firm focused on innovation financing, where I talked with hundreds of Parisian entrepreneurs, and this exact question — run it yourself or rent it from someone else — came up constantly. Open-weight models have made that question sharper than ever, so here’s how to actually think through it.

An open-weight model is a model whose trained parameters are published for anyone to download and run, without necessarily sharing the code or data used to train it. As the Open Source Initiative defines it, “Open Weights refer to the final weights and biases of a trained neural network.” You get the finished brain, not the recipe that built it. That distinction is exactly why open-weight models matter for this decision: because you can download the weights, you’re free to run them on your own hardware, on a cloud provider’s hardware or switch between the two, instead of being locked into one company’s API.

Self-hosting means running that open-weight model on infrastructure you control, whether that’s a GPU server sitting in your own office or a rented GPU virtual machine you fully manage. You pick the hardware, you install the software and you’re responsible for keeping it running.

Cloud means renting inference from a provider instead, whether that’s a managed endpoint hosting an open-weight model for you or a closed API you call over the internet. But cloud isn’t one single choice, because where that provider is headquartered changes what legal system governs your data. A U.S. cloud provider, even one running a data center inside the EU, remains bound by the CLOUD Act.

Here’s how it actually plays out. Below, I’ll call the winner between self-host and cloud on six specific fronts.

Self-hosting looks expensive on paper because you’re paying for a GPU whether you use it or not, but at high enough volume that fixed cost stops mattering. Cloudzy’s cost analysis explains that “self-hosting an open-weight model on a GPU VPS can beat a frontier API at high, sustained volume with good GPU utilization.” The catch is that most businesses never generate that kind of steady, maxed-out traffic. For anyone below that threshold, cloud wins on cost.

Running your own GPUs doesn’t just cost hardware money, it costs people, and that line item is easy to underestimate. Activepieces breaks down the real total cost of ownership and finds that “the payroll for these positions often exceeds the annual budget for the H100 GPUs they manage.” The engineers who keep a self-hosted stack alive frequently cost more than the chips they’re maintaining. Cloud wins here, because the provider absorbs that staffing burden for you.

For businesses handling sensitive or regulated data, who can legally compel access to your information matters as much as who can technically breach it. MassiveGRID lays out the jurisdiction problem plainly: “a U.S.-headquartered provider operating servers in the EU is still subject to the CLOUD Act,” while “a provider incorporated and operating entirely within the EU provides stronger protection against extraterritorial data access requests.” Self-hosting on your own hardware or choosing an EU-only cloud provider closes off that exposure entirely. Self-hosting, or EU cloud specifically, wins on legal exposure.

Demand for AI products rarely arrives in a straight line, and that’s where renting infrastructure pays off. Buzzclan defines the core benefit of cloud elasticity as “the ability to automatically adjust infrastructure capacity based on demand, helping businesses maintain performance without overprovisioning.” A self-hosted GPU server can’t grow on demand during a traffic spike or shrink back down when things go quiet, it just sits at whatever size you bought it at. Cloud wins on scalability.

Open-weight models exist precisely because businesses want to shape the model itself, not just prompt around its limits. A closed cloud API gives you a fixed model behind a fixed interface. Self-hosting wins on customization.

For a business selling into enterprise customers, a provider’s paperwork can matter as much as its performance. Google Cloud explains what its SOC 2 report actually verifies: “the SOC 2 reports are generated by an objective third party attesting to a set of assertions made by Google Cloud about its controls that are in place to protect customer data.” Building that same audited trail yourself, on your own servers, takes real time and specialized staff most startups don’t have. Cloud wins on compliance.

There’s no single winner here, and that’s the actual takeaway. Open-weight models made this a genuine choice instead of a forced one: The same model can run in a rented data center or on a box you own, and the right answer depends on which of these six factors matters most to your business right now.

If you’re regulated or handling sensitive data, lean self-host or EU cloud. If you’re scaling unpredictably or don’t want to hire an infrastructure team, lean cloud. Most businesses will end up doing both — cloud for the unpredictable parts, self-hosting for the parts that need full control — and that’s not indecision; it’s just matching the infrastructure to the actual argument that matters most in each case.

I’m an AI engineer and I’m currently building ChatMakr, an AI-powered platform that creates multi-agent chatbots in seconds, powered by open-weight models. I also spent time at a consulting firm focused on innovation financing, where I talked with hundreds of Parisian entrepreneurs, and this exact question — run it yourself or rent it from someone else — came up constantly. Open-weight models have made that question sharper than ever, so here’s how to actually think through it.

An open-weight model is a model whose trained parameters are published for anyone to download and run, without necessarily sharing the code or data used to train it. As the Open Source Initiative defines it, “Open Weights refer to the final weights and biases of a trained neural network.” You get the finished brain, not the recipe that built it. That distinction is exactly why open-weight models matter for this decision: because you can download the weights, you’re free to run them on your own hardware, on a cloud provider’s hardware or switch between the two, instead of being locked into one company’s API.

Self-hosting means running that open-weight model on infrastructure you control, whether that’s a GPU server sitting in your own office or a rented GPU virtual machine you fully manage. You pick the hardware, you install the software and you’re responsible for keeping it running.
